# The Attack on ISD (Gordon & Zemke, 2000)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
Gordon and Zemke's provocative Training magazine article launched a significant debate in the instructional design field by arguing that ISD (Instructional Systems Design) is flawed, out-of-date, and an obstacle to effective performance improvement. The authors contend that the ADDIE model is too slow, too rigid, and too focused on instructional solutions when non-instructional solutions are often more effective. The article catalyzed a years-long professional debate about whether ISD should be reformed or replaced, with responses appearing in subsequent issues and spawning the "attack on ISD" controversy in the field.

## Key Concepts
- ISD (Instructional Systems Design) critique
- ADDIE model limitations
- Rapid instructional design
- Non-instructional performance interventions
- HPT (Human Performance Technology) as ISD alternative

## Theoretical Framework
Practitioner critique of dominant paradigm; draws on practitioner experience and HPT principles to argue that academic ID models have failed to keep pace with organizational reality.

## Methods
Opinion/perspective piece combining practitioner experience, case examples, and selective literature review; published as a provocation intended to generate professional debate.

## Main Arguments
- ISD is too slow for modern organizational needs; the typical development timeline is incompatible with business timelines
- ADDIE's linear structure makes it unsuitable for real-world projects where analysis, design, and development overlap
- Many performance problems called "training needs" are actually organizational, motivational, or environmental in nature
- The field's attachment to ISD prevents adoption of more effective, agile approaches

## Limitations & Critiques
Critics argued Gordon and Zemke overstated the limitations of ISD by attacking a strawman version of the model; defenders noted that ISD, properly applied, is iterative and flexible; the article's provocative framing generated more heat than light in the subsequent debate.

# User Experience Design Professionals' Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence


## Abstract
Among creative professionals, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has sparked excitement over its capabilities and fear over unanticipated consequences. How does GenAI impact User Experience Design (UXD) practice, and are fears warranted? We interviewed 20 UX Designers, with diverse experience and across companies (startups to large enterprises). We probed them to characterize their practices, and sample their attitudes, concerns, and expectations. We found that experienced designers are confident in their originality, creativity, and empathic skills, and find GenAI’s role as assistive. They emphasized the unique human factors of “enjoyment” and “agency”, where humans remain the arbiters of “AI alignment’’. However, skill degradation, job replacement, and creativity exhaustion can adversely impact junior designers. We discuss implications for human-GenAI collaboration, specifically copyright and ownership, human creativity and agency, and AI literacy and access. Through the lens of responsible and participatory AI, we contribute a deeper understanding of GenAI fears and opportunities for UXD.

**DOI:** [10.1145/3613904.3642114](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642114)

## Summary
This study examines UX design professionals' perceptions of generative AI tools, documenting how practitioners across industry and agency contexts understand, evaluate, and integrate (or resist) AI in their UX workflows. Through interviews with practicing UX designers and researchers, the paper maps attitudes along dimensions of trust, skill relevance, and professional identity. Findings reveal significant heterogeneity: some practitioners see AI as a powerful collaborator that amplifies their judgment; others view it as a threat to the tacit knowledge that defines professional expertise. The paper calls for UX education and professional development to address AI integration head-on.

## Key Concepts
- UX professional AI perceptions and attitudes
- Trust calibration in AI-assisted UX work
- Tacit knowledge and professional expertise
- AI integration in UX workflows
- Professional identity and AI displacement anxiety

## Theoretical Framework
Professional cognition and expertise theory; technology acceptance model; human-AI collaboration framework; draws on UX practice literature and AI adoption research.

## Methods
Semi-structured interviews with UX design professionals across roles (designer, researcher, content strategist); thematic analysis of perceptions, adoption patterns, and resistance motivations.

## Main Arguments
- UX professionals hold complex, nuanced views of AI that resist simple adoption/resistance binary
- Trust in AI tools is conditional: high for repetitive or well-defined tasks, low for tasks requiring empathy, context sensitivity, and stakeholder negotiation
- Professional identity concerns are a significant — and underacknowledged — barrier to AI adoption in UX
- UX education and training programs need to address both technical AI skills and the identity challenges AI integration poses

# 'Clay to Play With': Generative AI Tools in UX and Industrial Design Practice


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1145/3643834.3661624](https://doi.org/10.1145/3643834.3661624)

## Summary
This paper explores industrial and UX designers' use of generative AI tools through the metaphor of "clay to play with" — positioning AI as a malleable, generative material that enables exploratory, low-stakes design experimentation. Through design research with practitioners in product and experience design contexts, the authors find that successful AI integration occurs when designers approach tools playfully and experimentally rather than instrumentally, treating AI outputs as starting points for design exploration rather than finished products. The paper argues for a materials-centered approach to understanding AI in design practice.

## Key Concepts
- AI as design material (not just a productivity tool)
- Playful and exploratory AI use
- Material encounters in design practice
- Generative AI in industrial design
- Experimentation and serendipity with AI

## Theoretical Framework
Material-centered design practice theory; draws on Ingold's material agency, Schön's reflective practice, and design studio research to frame AI as a new design material rather than a software tool.

## Methods
Design research with UX and industrial design practitioners; qualitative study combining design workshops, observation, and reflective interviews about AI material practice.

## Main Arguments
- Treating AI as a design material — something to manipulate, resist, and explore — produces richer outcomes than treating it as a productivity tool
- Playful experimentation with AI generates serendipitous discoveries that instrumentally-minded use misses
- The "clay" metaphor captures both the formability of AI outputs and the skill required to shape them toward design intent
- Design education should develop AI material literacy: understanding what this material can and cannot do, and how to develop craft with it

## Limitations & Critiques
The materials metaphor is productive but may not scale to all design contexts; the study's practitioner sample may represent early adopters; empirical evidence for learning outcomes from materials-based AI pedagogy is not yet established.

# Collaboration with Conversational AI Assistants for UX Evaluation: Questions and How to Ask Them


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1145/3544548.3581247](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581247)

## Summary
This paper investigates how conversational AI assistants can support UX evaluation activities, examining what kinds of questions UX practitioners ask AI systems during evaluations and which question forms elicit useful responses. Through user studies with UX practitioners conducting AI-assisted evaluations, the authors identify categories of productive questions (heuristic interpretation, guideline application, pattern recognition) and unproductive ones (requiring contextual judgment, stakeholder knowledge, or domain-specific nuance). The paper provides practical guidance for UX practitioners integrating conversational AI into evaluation workflows.

## Key Concepts
- Conversational AI for UX evaluation
- Question formulation and prompt design for UX
- Heuristic evaluation with AI assistance
- AI limitations in contextual judgment tasks
- UX evaluation workflow AI integration

## Theoretical Framework
Cognitive task analysis of UX evaluation; human-AI collaboration in professional practice; usability evaluation methods; draws on Nielsen's heuristic evaluation and AI-assisted work literature.

## Methods
User studies with UX practitioners conducting heuristic evaluations with AI assistance; think-aloud protocols; analysis of question types and response quality; qualitative coding of AI interaction patterns.

## Main Arguments
- AI assistants are most useful for UX evaluation when practitioners ask questions that can be answered from general UX knowledge (heuristics, principles, patterns)
- Questions requiring contextual knowledge about users, business constraints, or organizational culture produce unreliable AI responses
- Effective AI-assisted UX evaluation requires practitioners to develop new prompt literacy skills specific to evaluation tasks
- AI assistance is best positioned as a first-pass tool that practitioners then refine using domain expertise and contextual knowledge

## Limitations & Critiques
Study uses specific AI tools at a point in time; results may change as AI capabilities evolve; the sample of UX practitioners may skew toward those already comfortable with AI; evaluation contexts studied may not represent the full range of UX evaluation types.

# AI Hasn’t Fixed Teamwork, But It Shifted Collaborative


## Abstract
When AI entered the workplace, many believed it could re- shape teamwork as profoundly as it boosted individual pro- ductivity. Wo

## Summary
This paper examines how AI tools have changed collaborative dynamics in professional teams, arguing that while AI has not solved fundamental teamwork challenges (coordination, communication, trust), it has shifted where and how those challenges manifest. Through case studies and interviews with teams using AI tools, the authors document how AI changes the distribution of work within teams, the nature of handoffs, and the skills required for effective collaboration. The paper identifies new collaboration competencies required in AI-mediated team contexts.

## Key Concepts
- AI and team collaboration dynamics
- Work redistribution in AI-augmented teams
- Handoff challenges in human-AI-human workflows
- New collaboration competencies for AI-mediated work
- Trust and communication in AI-assisted teamwork

## Theoretical Framework
CSCW (Computer-Supported Cooperative Work); team cognition; human-AI teaming; draws on distributed cognition and coordination theory to analyze AI effects on team dynamics.

## Methods
Case studies of professional teams using AI tools; qualitative interviews with team members; observation of AI-mediated collaboration sessions; analysis of coordination patterns.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools shift where collaboration challenges occur rather than eliminating them: new friction points emerge around AI output evaluation and integration
- Teams develop new handoff practices for AI-generated outputs that require new competencies in quality assessment and contextual appropriateness evaluation
- Trust in AI varies within teams, creating asymmetric human-AI relationships that affect team coordination
- Effective AI-augmented teams develop shared norms around AI use that individual AI adoption cannot achieve

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study design limits generalizability; team AI tool use is rapidly evolving; the specific tools studied may not represent the landscape broadly; long-term effects on team collaboration culture are not tracked.

# AI Imaginaries: A Historical Timeline

> *A synthesis note drawing on vault papers and Adam Prumm's literature review "AI Imaginaries, Design Education, and the Transformation of Design Practice" (2025, unpublished).*

---

## What Is an Imaginary?

A **sociotechnical imaginary** is a collectively held vision of a desirable (or feared) social future made possible by a technology — visions that shape decisions, resource allocation, and policy *before* the technology matures. Jasanoff & Kim's foundational concept describes these as "collectively imagined forms of social life and social order reflected in the design and fulfillment of nation-specific scientific and/or technological projects."

Mager & Katzenbach (2021) sharpen this: imaginaries are **"multiple, contested, and commodified narratives"** — not neutral predictions, but political acts. They carry **performative power**: once an imagined future gains institutional momentum, it begins directing real priorities and behaviors regardless of whether it ever arrives. Stanusch et al. (2024) call these failures **"underperforming imaginaries"** — expected AI transformations that never materialize but still *reshape the labor force and reshape practice* in their wake.

Throughout AI's history, the word "imaginary" was rarely used. But the phenomenon was everywhere — in Wiener's proclamations about cybernetics, in Terminator sequels, in tech CEO keynotes, in faculty abstinence policies. This timeline traces those visions, who made them, what they predicted, and what they left behind.

**Adam Prumm's "imaginaries lifecycle"** (from his 2025 literature review) frames how these visions travel:

> Industry imaginaries → shape academic programs → shape student expectations → students carry them into the workforce → workforce expectations feed back into industry leadership

Misalignment accumulates at every transition in this cycle.

---

## Quick Reference Table

| Wave | Era | Dominant Imaginary | Who Proclaimed It | Key Fear |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | 1943–1966 | The Universal Machine — intelligence is information; machines will think | Scientists, military, mathematicians | Machines replacing human cognition at scale |
| **2** | 1966–1987 | The Expert & The Factory — AI encodes expert knowledge; blue-collar work at risk | AI researchers, industrial engineers, corporations | Factory job loss; AI winter disillusionment |
| **3** | 1987–2010 | The Safe Knowledge Worker — cognitive/creative work is automation-proof | Tech industry, economists, management theorists | System optimization, not human replacement |
| **4** | 2010–2019 | The Automation Panic — everything is now at risk, including white-collar work | Frey & Osborne, media, consultancies, Big Tech | Mass unemployment; 47% of jobs automated |
| **5** | 2019–present | Contested Imaginaries — tool, collaborator, or existential threat? | Practitioners, artists, researchers, executives | Creative displacement; who owns the future? |

---

## Wave 1: The Universal Machine (1943–1966)

### The Imaginary
**"Intelligence is information processing. Machines will think — and thinking is a universal, computable process."** *(Prumm, 2025)*

This imaginary was constructed almost entirely by scientists and mathematicians, largely working under military funding during and after WWII. Its core claim: that the brain is a machine, that machines can be brains, and that this equivalence would unlock control over any complex system — organisms, economies, societies.

### Scientific Proclamations
- **Norbert Wiener** — *Cybernetics: Control and Communication in Animal and Machine* (1948): coined "cybernetics" and argued that feedback, information, and control were universal principles governing biological and mechanical systems equally

# Competences for the Modern Designer: Systematic Literature Review (2026)


## Abstract
Higher education institutions offering education in design need to review their teaching content in relation to a changing society and digitalization. In emerging post-digital era higher education is in a state of change. Metacognitive skills and a focus on digitalized world’s competencies are becoming integral components of curricula in modern days. During the 21 st century emphasis in design education has been on design thinking, user-centered design, and the utilization of service designers. On the other hand, contemporary designers are expected to have the capacity to navigate complexity and address wicked problems. Designers are now being called upon to contribute to complex problems, in a highly decentralized and heterogeneous contexts within development processes that are increasingly connected. The change in the field of design and in the professional definition is so rapid that there is no curriculum that can predict the future. This raises two research questions: What are future competences for designers? How these changes should be considered in the design education? The scope of this systematic literature review encompasses scholarly works published in international peer-reviewed academic journals during the period spanning from 1.1.2018 to 31.3.2024. The primary objective is to discern evolving perceptions of the design profession in the future and to identify the key competencies that emerging designers should adeptly master as they navigate the landscape of a digitalized working environment.

**DOI:** [10.1177/14740222251342646](https://doi.org/10.1177/14740222251342646)

## Summary
This 2026 systematic literature review examines the competences required for modern designers, synthesizing recent research to update understanding of design expertise in contexts where AI tools have become pervasive. The review identifies core stable competencies (empathy, systems thinking, conceptual development, iteration) alongside new AI-mediated competencies (AI direction, quality evaluation of AI outputs, ethical AI use). The paper argues that the core of design expertise is shifting from production skills toward meta-cognitive and judgment competencies that complement AI capabilities.

## Key Concepts
- Modern designer competencies framework
- Systematic literature review methodology
- Stable vs. AI-emergent competences in design
- Metacognitive design competences
- Design judgment in AI-mediated practice

## Theoretical Framework
Competency-based education; design expertise research; systematic review methodology; draws on design education and professional competency literature from 2010-2026 to identify shifts in the competency landscape.

## Methods
Systematic literature review following PRISMA protocol; analysis of design competency frameworks from design education, professional organization, and empirical research sources; coding and synthesis of competency categories and their AI-era evolution.

## Main Arguments
- Core design competencies centered on empathy, systems thinking, and conceptual development remain stable and central in the AI era
- New AI-specific competencies (directing AI, evaluating AI quality, ethical AI deployment) are now necessary additions to the design competency framewor

# Using Generative AI Tools in Collaborative UX Design Courses


## Abstract
Artificial Intelligence and their derived Generative technologies are playing a cru - cial role in many applications that involve an active collaboration among machine assistants and human users. That is the case for User Experience courses that al - lowed students and instructors work together with Generative Artificial Intelligence tools to produce a collaborative design. The main purpose of this research consisted in reviewing several stages in design tasks that could take advantage of Artificial Intelligence tools by boosting a prompt-based conversation among instructors and students. Results obtained through the use of these tools demonstrated their huge potential in facilitating co-creative tasks. In this context, a first cohort of students was able to collaborate on the ideation of User Experience projects by exchanging prompts to define persona profiles and checking their suitability. A second cohort was involved in the joint assessment of testing mockups related

**DOI:** [10.1007/s40593-025-00518-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00518-1)

## Summary
This paper examines how design educators integrated generative AI tools into collaborative UX design courses, documenting the pedagogical strategies, student experiences, and learning outcomes that emerged. The study finds that AI tools can enhance collaborative ideation and rapid prototyping while creating new tensions around individual contribution, creative ownership, and skill development. The authors develop recommendations for educators on how to structure AI-assisted collaborative design projects to maximize learning without undermining the collaborative skills that UX education seeks to develop.

## Key Concepts
- Generative AI in UX design education
- Collaborative design with AI tools
- Pedagogical scaffolding for AI-assisted work
- Group creative process and AI mediation
- Assessment in AI-assisted collaborative courses

## Theoretical Framework
Collaborative learning theory; design pedagogy; CSCW perspectives on AI-mediated teamwork; draws on project-based learning frameworks.

## Methods
Qualitative study of multiple UX design courses integrating AI tools; student surveys, focus groups, and design artifact analysis; instructor reflective practice documentation.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools change the division of labor in collaborative design projects in ways that require new pedagogical scaffolding
- Without explicit instruction, students tend to use AI to bypass collaborative negotiation rather than to enhance it
- Effective AI-assisted collaboration requires structured activities that preserve human-to-human creative dialogue
- Assessment must evolve to evaluate the quality of AI direction and curation, not just final design outputs

## Limitations & Critiques
Study conducted during rapid AI tool evolution; findings may not transfer to different course structures or student populations; long-term effects on collaborative design skill development are not tracked.

# Artificial Intelligence and Work Transformations Integrating Sensemaking and Workplace Learning Perspectives

# Study Partner Note: AI and Work Transformations

## Summary
This paper explores how organizational members make sense of AI adoption and how perceived AI features trigger sensemaking processes that shape workplace learning modes. The study matters because it addresses a gap in understanding how organizations navigate the uncertainties and organizational changes posed by AI implementation, moving beyond technology-centric dichotomies to examine socio-technical dynamics.

## Key Concepts
- **Sensemaking**: The cognitive process by which organizational members interpret and respond to AI adoption
- **Exploitative vs. Explorative Learning Paths**: Two distinct workplace learning trajectories triggered by different AI feature perceptions
- **Abstract vs. Concrete Features of AI**: Technology characteristics that differentially activate sensemaking processes
- **Socio-technical Processes**: The integration of technical systems with social and organizational factors in technology adoption
- **Workplace Learning Trajectories**: Pathways of organizational learning shaped by initial interpretations of AI technology

## Theoretical Framework
The authors combine sensemaking theory (Weick, 1995) with organizational learning perspectives to analyze how initial interpretations of AI trigger different workplace learning modes. This socio-technical lens moves beyond purely technical or human-centric framings to examine the interplay between technology features and organizational interpretation.

## Methods
The study employed an exploratory qualitative approach using 23 focus groups across four large Swedish manufacturing companies, capturing participants' imaginative ideas and reflections on AI adoption. Data were analyzed using the Gioia method, a systematic qualitative technique for developing conceptual categories from raw data.

## Main Arguments
- Abstract AI features (e.g., general automation concepts) trigger sensemaking that leads to exploitative learning paths, potentially narrowing organizational responses
- Concrete AI features (e.g., specific use cases, tangible applications) activate sensemaking processes that enable explorative learning paths
- Socio-technical processes—not technology alone—are crucial drivers of successful AI adoption trajectories
- Initial sensemaking processes shape downstream organizational learning and change outcomes

## Limitations & Critiques
The study is limited to manufacturing contexts in Sweden and relies on focus group data, which may reflect aspirational rather than actual workplace experiences with AI. The paper also does not deeply examine how power dynamics, organizational hierarchies, or individual differences influence sensemaking processes across organizational members.

# Artificial Intelligence as a Tool for Individual and Collaborative Creativity in Design Education


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1016/j.yjoc.2024.100079](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yjoc.2024.100079)

Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the design process is a growing area of research interest. Three years after its public launch in 2022, AI has already established itself as the most disruptive tool revolutionizing how designers conceptualize, iterate and innovate. As AI technologies continue to evolve, it is pertinent that design students are acquainted with the potential of the technology and how it can be integrated in their professional practice. The objective of this paper is to explore the role of AI as a conceptualization and research tool in interior design. We aim to examine its effectiveness in enhancing the ideation process and facilitating collaboration and knowledge sharing in intercultural design teams. The case study presented is a collaborative online international learning project (COIL) with the participation of

## Summary
This paper investigates generative AI as a tool for supporting both individual and collaborative creativity in design education, examining how students and faculty use AI during ideation, iteration, and concept development. Through case studies of AI-integrated design courses, the authors find that AI tools open new creative possibilities and lower barriers to visual ideation, but also raise concerns about the homogenization of student work and the erosion of individual creative voice. The paper argues for pedagogical frameworks that cultivate students' capacity to use AI creatively while preserving distinctive design perspectives.

## Key Concepts
- AI as creativity tool (individual and collaborative)
- Design ideation with generative AI
- Creative homogenization risk
- Individual creative voice in AI-mediated design
- Collaborative creativity with AI mediation

## Theoretical Framework
Creativity theory; collaborative cognition; design education pedagogy; draws on componential model of creativity (Amabile) and social creativity frameworks.

## Methods
Multiple case studies of design courses integrating AI for creative tasks; qualitative analysis of student work, reflections, and interviews about AI's role in their creative process.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools significantly lower the barrier to visual ideation, enabling students to generate more concepts faster
- Collaborative creativity benefits from AI when it serves as a shared ideation partner rather than an individual shortcut
- Without pedagogical intervention, AI use tends to converge student outputs toward aesthetically similar results
- Design education must develop students' capacity to use AI creatively — including knowing when not to use it

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study design limits generalizability; the homogenization risk may be tool-specific and evolve as AI models improve; measuring "individual creative voice" empirically remains challenging.

# Standards and Ethics in Human Performance Technology (Guerra, 2006)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
Guerra's chapter on standards and ethics in HPT examines the professional obligations of performance technologists, reviewing ISPI's performance standards and the ethical principles that should guide HPT practice. The chapter addresses tensions between client demands, organizational goals, and practitioner ethics, arguing that HPT professionals must maintain independent judgment about the appropriateness and ethics of interventions. It positions ethics not as an add-on but as integral to competent HPT practice.

## Key Concepts
- ISPI performance standards (10 standards framework)
- Ethical principles in performance consulting
- Client-practitioner relationships and conflicts of interest
- Competence and scope of practice
- Confidentiality and informed consent in organizational settings

## Theoretical Framework
Professional ethics framework applied to HPT; draws on codes of professional conduct from related fields (consulting, psychology, organizational development) to develop HPT-specific ethical guidance.

## Methods
Normative analysis of professional standards documents; case-based reasoning about ethical dilemmas in HPT practice; comparative review of ethics frameworks across related professions.

## Main Arguments
- Performance technologists must distinguish between what clients want and what is ethically appropriate to provide
- ISPI's standards provide a framework for competent practice, but ethical judgment is required when standards conflict
- HPT practitioners have dual obligations to client organizations and to the individuals whose performance they seek to improve
- The field's applied nature does not exempt it from the ethical obligations common to other helping professions

## Limitations & Critiques
The chapter reflects the ISPI institutional perspective; independent consultants and in-house practitioners face different ethical pressures not fully addressed; the treatment of cultural and diversity considerations is limited.

# Understanding the Past, Present, and Future of Design Fictions (Muller & Fiesler, CHI 2020)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1145/3334480.3375168](https://doi.org/10.1145/3334480.3375168)

## Summary
Muller and Fiesler's CHI 2020 workshop summary documents a collaborative inquiry into the past, present, and future of design fictions — speculative design artifacts that explore possible and preferable futures to stimulate reflection, debate, and ethical inquiry. The workshop surfaces tensions in design fiction practice: whether it is primarily artistic, analytical, or activist; how it relates to speculative design and critical design; and how it can be made more inclusive and diverse. The summary synthesizes emerging consensus and open questions for the design fiction research community.

## Key Concepts
- Design fiction (artifacts from speculative futures)
- Speculative design and critical design
- Diegetic prototypes
- Futures literacy and ethical foresight
- Participatory and inclusive futures

## Theoretical Framework
Speculative design tradition (Dunne & Raby); science fiction prototyping; futures studies; draws on Sterling's design fiction concept and critical design to situate the workshop's conceptual scope.

## Methods
Workshop summary; collaborative sense-making across ~30 design fiction researchers and practitioners; synthesis of position papers and discussion sessions.

## Main Arguments
- Design fiction is a diverse practice with multiple legitimate goals (exploration, critique, participation, provocation)
- The field lacks consensus on methodological standards and evaluation criteria, which both enables creativity and limits scholarly rigor
- More attention is needed to whose futures are centered in design fiction and who is excluded from speculative exercises
- Design fiction has growing relevance for AI ethics, policy, and HCI research as a tool for anticipating sociotechnical consequences

## Limitations & Critiques
As a workshop summary, the document reflects the perspectives of a relatively homogeneous research community; the lack of methodological standards noted in the workshop has not yet been fully resolved in subsequent literature.

## Summary
This paper presents a SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) analysis of generative AI tools in instructional design practice. Published in TechTrends (2024), it examines how instructional designers can leverage GenAI while navigating its limitations and risks.

## Key Concepts
- **Generative AI in ID practice**: How tools like ChatGPT can assist at various stages of the instructional design process (analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation)
- **SWOT framework**: Structured evaluation of GenAI — strengths (efficiency, ideation support), weaknesses (accuracy, bias), opportunities (personalization, scalability), threats (over-reliance, ethical issues)
- **ADDIE integration**: Examining where GenAI fits within the traditional ADDIE model stages

## Theoretical Framework
Grounded in instructional design theory and the ADDIE model; uses strategic management's SWOT analysis as an evaluative lens applied to emerging technology adoption in professional practice.

## Methods
Conceptual/analytical paper applying the SWOT framework to synthesize existing literature and practitioner knowledge about generative AI capabilities and limitations in instructional design contexts.

## Main Arguments
1. GenAI offers genuine productivity gains for instructional designers, particularly in content drafting, brainstorming, and rapid prototyping of learning materials
2. Significant weaknesses exist around factual accuracy, hallucination, and the need for subject-matter expert review — GenAI cannot replace ID expertise
3. The greatest opportunity lies in personalizing learning experiences at scale, which was previously impractical
4. The primary threat is uncritical over-reliance that erodes core instructional design competencies and introduces unreviewed errors into learning materials

# Optimizing Employee Roles in the Era of Generative AI


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1080/23311886.2025.2476737](https://doi.org/10.1080/23311886.2025.2476737)

## Summary
This paper examines how generative AI is reshaping employee roles in organizations through a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) analysis of co-creation dynamics, proposing an optimization framework for role allocation in AI-integrated work environments. Published in Cogent Social Sciences, the paper addresses the managerial challenge of deciding which tasks and roles should be assigned to humans, AI, or human-AI co-creation teams, using quantitative MCDM methods to identify optimal configurations.

## Key Concepts
- Employee role optimization under GenAI
- Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) for role allocation
- Human-AI co-creation dynamics
- Organizational role reconfiguration with AI

## Theoretical Framework
Operations research and organizational management frameworks; MCDM methodology applied to the problem of optimizing human and AI role configurations in work organizations.

## Methods
Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) quantitative analysis; models different co-creation configurations (human-only, AI-only, hybrid) against multiple criteria; published in Cogent Social Sciences.

## Main Arguments
- Employee role optimization in AI-integrated organizations requires systematic multi-criteria analysis
- Different task types warrant different human-AI configurations — no universal optimal solution
- Co-creation dynamics between humans and AI are context-dependent and must be empirically assessed

# Integrating AI into Instructional Design: A Pedagogical Framework (Contemporary Ed Tech, 2025)


## Abstract
This article explores the theoretical and instructional underpinnings of distance learning with a specific focus on foreign language education. It examines constructivist, connectivist, and humanistic foundations, highlighting pedagogical advantages and limitations. Additionally, the article outlines effective instructional design models, including ADDIE and SAM, supported by cognitive theories and Bloom's taxonomy. Empirical data from global and regional contexts reinforce the practical relevance of the theoretical framework. Illustrative tables and figures are included to support the comparative and conceptual analysis.c

**DOI:** [10.30935/cedtech/16433](https://doi.org/10.30935/cedtech/16433)

## Summary
This 2025 paper in Contemporary Educational Technology proposes a pedagogical framework for integrating AI into instructional design practice, addressing the gap between available AI tools and principled frameworks for using them in ID work. The framework organizes AI integration around the core activities of instructional design (needs analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation) and specifies where AI assistance adds value versus where human judgment is indispensable. The paper argues that instructional designers need frameworks grounded in learning theory, not just technical capability, to integrate AI responsibly.

## Key Concepts
- AI integration framework for instructional design
- ADDIE model and AI tool integration
- Learning theory-grounded AI use in ID
- Human judgment vs. AI assistance in instructional design
- Responsible AI adoption in educational technology

## Theoretical Framework
Instructional design theory; ADDIE and SAM models; AI integration frameworks; draws on established ID theory to provide principled guidance rather than ad hoc tool adoption.

## Methods
Framework development; literature synthesis of AI capabilities and ID process requirements; case examples of AI integration at each ADDIE phase.

## Main Arguments
- Instructional designers need theory-grounded frameworks for AI integration, not just tool tutorials or capability inventories
- AI adds most value in ID at the development and evaluation phases where pattern recognition and data analysis capabilities are relevant
- Human judgment remains indispensable at needs analysis and design phases where contextual understanding, stakeholder relationships, and value choices cannot be delegated
- The framework enables deliberate AI integration that preserves instructional designers' professional expertise rather than replacing it

## Limitations & Critiques
Framework is primarily prescriptive without comprehensive empirical validation; AI capabilities at each ADDIE phase are evolving rapidly; the framework may be more applicable to large-scale ID contexts than rapid or agile development contexts.

# Content Analysis

## Overview
Content analysis is a systematic, replicable technique for compressing texts into meaningful categories. Herring's Web Content Analysis (WebCA) extends classical content analysis to computer-mediated communication, treating the web as a medium with distinct structural, social, and textual dimensions. It is distinguished from discourse analysis by its emphasis on explicit, pre-specified coding schemes applied to observable message features rather than the interpretation of rhetorical strategies.

# Developing Students' Instrumental Design Judgment (MurdochKitt et al., DECIPHER 2018)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
MurdochKitt, Culén, and Mainsah's conference paper investigates how design students develop instrumental design judgment — the capacity to make principled choices about design tools and methods in context. Using a constructivist pedagogical framework, they examine how explicit instruction in judgment development differs from tacit acquisition through studio experience alone. The paper argues that design education must move beyond method instruction to cultivate the meta-cognitive capacities that allow designers to evaluate and select among methods appropriately.

## Key Concepts
- Instrumental design judgment
- Design method selection and evaluation
- Constructivist design pedagogy
- Metacognition in design education
- Design tool literacy

## Theoretical Framework
Stolterman and Nelson's foundational/instrumental design theory; constructivist learning; metacognitive development in professional education.

## Methods
Design pedagogy research; case study from a design course at Oslo Metropolitan University; qualitative analysis of student reflections and design process documentation.

## Main Arguments
- Design methods are tools; knowing when and why to use them is judgment that must be explicitly cultivated
- Students often learn methods as rituals without understanding the conditions under which each method is appropriate
- Pedagogical interventions that make judgment explicit produce more adaptable designers than method-focused instruction alone
- Evaluation of method appropriateness requires knowledge of the design situation, not just the method

## Limitations & Critiques
Single-course case study limits generalizability; student population at a single Scandinavian institution may not reflect global design education diversity; the framework for assessing judgment development needs further operationalization.

This LNAI (Lecture Notes in AI) volume edited by Degen and Ntoa presents collected research on artificial intelligence in human-computer interaction from the 2025 HCI International conference. The volume covers advances in AI-mediated interaction design, intelligent interface systems, conversational AI UX, and AI evaluation methods. As an edited conference proceedings volume, it represents the current state of AI-HCI research practice, providing a snapshot of where the field is directing its attention in the integration of AI capabilities with human-centered interaction design.

Human-computer interaction; AI systems design; user experience research; the volume encompasses multiple theoretical frameworks from contributing authors across AI and HCI domains.

## Methods
Edited proceedings volume; peer-reviewed conference papers presenting empirical, design, and theoretical contributions to AI-HCI at the 2025 HCI International conference.

## Main Arguments
- AI-HCI research in 2025 is focused on making AI systems more explainable, controllable, and aligned with user mental models
- Conversational AI and LLM-based interfaces represent the dominant emerging interaction paradigm requiring new HCI frameworks
- Evaluation of AI-infused systems requires new metrics that account for dynamic, adaptive behavior not captured by traditional usability measures
- Human-centered AI design must address trust, transparency, and user agency as core design requirements, not afterthoughts

## Limitations & Critiques
Conference proceedings format means individual contributions vary in scope and rigor; as an edited volume, it lacks the synthesizing framework of a monograph; the 2025 snapshot will date as AI-HCI research advances.

# Design Thinking and Agile Design


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1007/978-1-4842-6461-4_10](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-6461-4_10)

## Summary
This paper examines the relationship between Design Thinking — a human-centered, divergent-convergent problem-solving methodology — and Agile software development — an iterative, sprint-based development approach. The authors argue that while the two frameworks are complementary in principle (both emphasize iteration, user feedback, and embracing change), they can conflict in practice due to different timelines, team structures, and validation standards. The paper offers a synthesis model for integrating Design Thinking's front-end exploration with Agile's development cycles.

## Key Concepts
- Design Thinking (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test)
- Agile software development (sprints, backlog, user stories)
- Double diamond process model
- Human-centered design in software contexts
- Sprint 0 and discovery phases

## Theoretical Framework
Process methodology synthesis; draws on IDEO's design thinking framework, the British Design Council's double diamond, and Agile manifesto principles to identify complementarities and tensions.

## Methods
Comparative framework analysis; case study of integrated Design Thinking-Agile teams; practitioner interviews and literature review.

## Main Arguments
- Design Thinking excels at problem framing and user research; Agile excels at efficient, iterative delivery — neither alone is sufficient
- The most common friction occurs when Agile sprint timelines are too short for meaningful design exploration
- A hybrid approach requires organizational commitment to "Sprint 0" or "Discovery" phases before development sprints begin
- Shared vocabulary between designers and developers is essential for effective integration

## Limitations & Critiques
Integration success depends heavily on organizational context and team maturity; the synthesis model may work differently in product vs. service design contexts; "Design Thinking" itself is a contested and varied practice across organizations.

# Designer Experiences and Perspectives on the Role of Generative AI in Industrial Design (SÃƒÂ¼ner-Pla-CerdÃƒÂ  et al., AI & Society 2025)

## Summary
SÃ¼ner-Pla-CerdÃ  and colleagues' 2025 open-access study in AI & Society documents industrial designers' experiences with and perspectives on generative AI tools in professional practice, revealing a complex landscape of enthusiasm, anxiety, identity renegotiation, and practical adaptation. The study uses rich qualitative data from practicing industrial designers to examine how AI is reshaping design workflows, client relationships, and professional identity. The paper contributes an empirically grounded account of how a specific design discipline â€” industrial design â€” is processing AI's arrival.

## Key Concepts
- Industrial design practice and generative AI
- Professional identity in AI-transformed practice
- Workflow adaptation and AI integration
- Client-designer relationships with AI mediation
- AI anxiety and creative ownership concerns

## Theoretical Framework
Sociology of professions; professional identity theory; human-AI collaboration; draws on design practice literature and organizational sociology to frame practitioners' responses to AI disruption.

## Methods
Qualitative study; in-depth interviews with practicing industrial designers across career stages; thematic analysis of AI experience, adoption, and identity narratives.

## Main Arguments
- Industrial designers experience AI as both a capability amplifier and an identity threat simultaneously
- Workflow adaptation is already widespread: AI is being used for concept generation, client presentation, and manufacturing visualization
- Designers who find ways to articulate distinctive human value (cultural context, embodied material knowledge, client empathy) report less identity threat
- The client relationship is being renegotiated: AI-enabled faster delivery changes client expectations and pricing dynamics in ways designers are still navigating

## Limitations & Critiques
Qualitative sample may not represent the full diversity of industrial design practice globally; findings reflect a moment of rapid change and may evolve quickly; the interview context may elicit more reflective responses than designers' actual daily experience.

# Designing Instructional Strategies: A Cognitive Perspective (Silber & Foshay)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
Silber and Foshay's chapter provides a systematic account of instructional strategy selection from a cognitive science perspective, arguing that effective instructional design requires matching strategy choices to the cognitive demands of the target learning outcomes. The authors synthesize research on elaboration theory, component display theory, and cognitive load theory to offer a principled framework for making instructional decisions. The work bridges theory and practice by translating cognitive psychology findings into actionable design guidance.

## Key Concepts
- Instructional strategy (macro vs. micro strategies)
- Cognitive load theory (Sweller)
- Elaboration theory (Reigeluth)
- Component display theory (Merrill)
- Learning outcome types (declarative knowledge, procedural skills, problem solving)

## Theoretical Framework
Cognitive instructional design theory; integrates multiple cognitive psychology models to argue that instructional strategy must be derived systematically from analysis of the learning task's cognitive demands.

## Methods
Conceptual synthesis of empirical cognitive science research and established instructional design models; chapter in the Handbook of Improving Performance in the Workplace.

## Main Arguments
- Instructional strategies must align with the cognitive demands of the performance outcome, not just the subject matter domain
- Different content types (facts, concepts, procedures, principles) require different instructional approaches
- Cognitive load management is a primary driver of effective instruction for complex skills
- Front-end analysis (task and learner analysis) must precede strategy selection

## Limitations & Critiques
The cognitive approach can underemphasize motivational, affective, and social dimensions of learning; the framework assumes relatively stable, well-defined learning objectives which may not apply to creative or ill-structured domains.

# Industrial Designers in UX Practice: Motivations, Professionalization, and Designer Identity (Süner-Pla-Cerdà et al., 2023)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1162/desi_a_00715](https://doi.org/10.1162/desi_a_00715)

Abstract Our article discusses the insights from original research conducted with design practitioners to better understand the experiences of industrial design graduates as they are adopting new professional roles in user experience (UX) affiliated positions. We utilize narrative identity work as the theoretical frame to interpret the legitimation strategies of industrial designers while grounding their motivations, perceived competence, and fitness to a UX position. Such narratives support our arguments on the conscious efforts of designers toward the construction of a professional designer identity, which is stimulated by this role change.

## Summary
Süner-Pla-Cerdà, Bohemia, and colleagues' 2023 Design Issues paper examines how industrial designers navigate entry into and practice within user experience design, documenting the motivations, professionalization dynamics, and identity negotiations involved. Through interviews with industrial designers working in UX roles, the paper finds that lateral entrants from industrial design bring distinctive competencies (material thinking, form development, manufacturing context) that enrich UX practice while creating professional identity tensions with UX-native practitioners. The paper contributes to understanding of design discipline boundary permeability and professional identity in multidisciplinary design work.

## Key Concepts
- Industrial designers in UX practice
- Lateral entry and professional identity
- Industrial design competencies in UX contexts
- Professional boundary negotiation
- Designer identity in multidisciplinary practice

## Theoretical Framework
Sociology of professions; professional identity theory; boundary crossing in design disciplines; draws on Abbott's system of professions and occupational identity research.

## Methods
Semi-structured interviews with industrial designers working in UX roles; thematic analysis of motivation, professionalization, and identity narratives; comparative analysis of industrial design and UX-native perspectives.

## Main Arguments
- Industrial designers bring distinctive competencies to UX practice that complement UX-trained practitioners' skill sets
- Professional identity negotiations are a significant dimension of lateral entry: industrial designers must articulate their distinctive value in UX language
- The permeability of design discipline boundaries reflects the field's evolving nature and creates opportunities for cross-fertilization
- UX practice is enriched by diverse disciplinary entry paths, though professional communities of practice need frameworks for integrating different design epistemologies

## Limitations & Critiques
Sample limited to Spanish and UK industrial designers; the findings may reflect specific national design education traditions; the professionalization dynamics described may be specific to mid-career transitions rather than new graduates.

## Summary
Clark and Mayer's textbook "e-Learning and the Science of Instruction" applies cognitive learning science principles to the design of e-learning materials, translating research on multimedia learning into practical guidelines for instructional designers. The book introduces principles such as the coherence principle, signaling principle, contiguity principle, and modality principle, each grounded in Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning. It is the foundational applied reference for evidence-based e-learning design.

## Key Concepts
- Multimedia learning principles (coherence, signaling, contiguity, modality, etc.)
- Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (Mayer)
- Evidence-based e-learning design
- Worked examples and practice principles

## Theoretical Framework
Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML); grounded in cognitive psychology research on working memory, dual-channel processing, and schema formation in multimedia environments.

## Methods
Applied synthesis of cognitive science research for instructional design practice; translates experimental findings into design guidelines; textbook format with principles, examples, and case studies.

## Main Arguments
- Effective e-learning design must account for cognitive architecture — working memory limits and dual-channel processing
- Eleven evidence-based multimedia principles guide effective e-learning design
- Many common e-learning practices (e.g., adding background music, decorative graphics) are counterproductive
- The science of instruction can be reliably applied to improve learner outcomes in digital learning environments

# Educational Technology AECT Definition and Terminology (Januszewski Molenda 2008)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1111/j.1467-8535.2008.00925_4.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2008.00925_4.x)

## Summary
Januszewski and Molenda's AECT definitional work establishes the 2008 official definition of educational technology as "the study and ethical practice of facilitating learning and improving performance by creating, using, and managing appropriate technological processes and resources." The text unpacks each element of this definition, tracing the historical development of the field from visual instruction to audiovisual communication to the broader conception of instructional technology. The definition grounds the field's professional identity and scope.

## Key Concepts
- Educational technology definition (AECT 2008)
- Facilitation vs. instruction (shift in conceptualization)
- Performance improvement alongside learning
- Ethical practice as a core professional obligation
- Technological processes and resources (broad conception)

## Theoretical Framework
Professional/disciplinary definitional framework; draws on the historical evolution of AECT's prior definitions (1963, 1972, 1977, 1994) to situate the 2008 revision within the field's intellectual development.

## Methods
Conceptual and historical analysis; committee-based definition development typical of professional association standard-setting; comparative analysis of prior AECT definitions.

## Main Arguments
- The field has expanded from focusing narrowly on audiovisual media to encompassing all processes and resources for learning and performance improvement
- "Ethical practice" was explicitly added in 2008, reflecting the profession's responsibility beyond technical effectiveness
- Facilitating learning (not just delivering instruction) represents a student-centered epistemological commitment
- The definition must balance precision (guiding practice) with breadth (capturing the field's full scope)

## Limitations & Critiques
Definitional consensus documents necessarily smooth over genuine theoretical disagreements within the field; the 2008 definition has been critiqued for underemphasizing sociocultural and critical perspectives on technology.

# Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology (Jonassen et al., 1996)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1111/j.1467-8535.2004.00409_15.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2004.00409_15.x)

## Summary
Jonassen, Driscoll, and colleagues' 1996 Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology represents a comprehensive synthesis of the field's foundational research, covering learning theory, instructional design, media and technology research, diffusion of innovation, and evaluation methods. As the first major research handbook in the field, it established educational communications and technology (ECT) as a serious research discipline with its own methods, phenomena, and theoretical traditions. The handbook's breadth makes it a foundational reference for understanding the intellectual roots of educational technology and instructional design.

## Key Concepts
- Educational communications and technology (ECT) as a field
- Foundational research paradigms in educational technology
- Learning theory and instructional design connections
- Media comparison research and media effects
- Diffusion of innovation in educational technology

## Theoretical Framework
Encyclopedic meta-theoretical framework; draws on behavioral, cognitive, and constructivist learning theory; systems theory; communication theory; and empirical educational research traditions.

## Methods
Edited handbook synthesizing research across ECT's foundational areas; chapter-length reviews of research programs by field experts; no single primary methodology.

## Main Arguments
- Educational communications and technology has developed a distinctive research tradition worthy of systematic documentation
- The field's research spans from psychological learning theory to sociology of technology diffusion and system design
- Multiple theoretical perspectives are necessary to address the full range of ECT phenomena
- Empirical research methods must be chosen to match the phenomena being studied rather than applying a single paradigm uniformly

## Limitations & Critiques
As a 1996 volume, it predates the internet era, digital learning environments, and contemporary AI — primarily of historical and foundational value; the field has evolved significantly since publication.

# The Role of Student Motivation in Integrating AI into Web Design Education (2024)


## Abstract
Amidst the current wave studies of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, this longitudinal case study, spanning Spring 2023 to Spring 2024, delves into the integration of AI in the UI/UX web design classroom. By introducing both text-based and image-based AI tools to students with varying levels of skill in introductory web design and user experience (UX) courses, the study observed a significant enhancement in student creative capabilities and project outcomes. The utilization of text-based generators markedly improved writing efficiency and coding, while image-based tools facilitated better ideation and color selection. These findings underscore the potential to augment traditional educational methods, providing students with nov

**DOI:** [10.59400/fes.v2i2.1242](https://doi.org/10.59400/fes.v2i2.1242)

## Summary
This 2024 paper examines the role of student motivation in the integration of AI tools into web design education, investigating how motivational factors (intrinsic interest, extrinsic incentive, and self-efficacy) predict AI adoption patterns and learning outcomes in web design courses. The study finds that self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation are the strongest predictors of productive AI use, while extrinsic motivation alone correlates with superficial AI adoption. The paper argues for motivationally-informed instructional design when integrating AI into web design education.

## Key Concepts
- Student motivation and AI adoption in web design
- Self-efficacy and AI tool use
- Intrinsic vs. extrinsic motivation in technology-integrated learning
- Web design education and AI integration
- Motivationally-informed instructional design

## Theoretical Framework
Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan); technology acceptance model; self-efficacy theory (Bandura); draws on educational motivation research and AI adoption literature.

## Methods
Survey study with web design students in AI-integrated courses; motivational assessment instruments; correlation and regression analysis linking motivation variables to AI adoption behaviors and learning outcome measures.

## Main Arguments
- Self-efficacy is the strongest motivational predictor of productive AI use in web design learning
- Students with high intrinsic motivation use AI as a learning tool; those with only extrinsic motivation tend to use AI to bypass learning
- Instructional design should build student self-efficacy for AI tasks before expecting productive AI integration
- Motivational supports (choice, relevance, mastery framing) can improve AI integration outcomes in web design courses

## Limitations & Critiques
Cross-sectional survey design; motivation-behavior relationships are correlational not causal; the specific web design context may not generalize to other design disciplines; self-reported motivation measures have reliability limitations.

# Foundational and Instrumental Design Theory (Stolterman & Nelson)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1162/desi_a_00107](https://doi.org/10.1162/desi_a_00107)

## Summary
Stolterman and Nelson's theoretical framework distinguishes between foundational design theory (explaining what design is) and instrumental design theory (prescribing how to design). They argue that design as a field has been dominated by instrumental approaches at the expense of foundational inquiry, producing a field that knows how to do design but struggles to articulate what design fundamentally is. The work calls for a more philosophically grounded design theory that can speak to design's nature, purpose, and relationship to human judgment.

## Key Concepts
- Foundational design theory (ontological/explanatory)
- Instrumental design theory (prescriptive/methodological)
- Design judgment and phronesis (practical wisdom)
- Ultimate particular (the specific, situated design outcome)
- Design as a synthetic, intentional human activity

## Theoretical Framework
Philosophy of design; draws on Aristotle's practical reasoning (phronesis), phenomenology, and pragmatism to argue that design involves judgment that cannot be fully systematized or codified into rules.

## Methods
Conceptual analysis and philosophical argumentation; no empirical component; synthesizes philosophy of practice, design theory, and systems theory.

## Main Arguments
- The dominance of instrumental design theory has obscured the fundamentally judgmental and value-laden nature of design
- Every design outcome is an "ultimate particular" — uniquely situated and not fully generalizable
- Foundational theory is needed to understand what makes design good, not just how to do it efficiently
- Design education must cultivate practical wisdom, not just method fluency

## Limitations & Critiques
Highly abstract and philosophical; critics note the framework may be difficult to operationalize in design education or practice; the distinction between foundational and instrumental may be less stable in practice than the theory suggests.

# Generative AI and Creative Work: Narratives, Values, and Impacts (Caramiaux et al., Microsoft Research, 2023)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
Caramiaux and colleagues at Microsoft Research and partner institutions present a qualitative study of how creative professionals across disciplines (visual artists, musicians, writers, designers) narrate their experiences with generative AI, examining the values at stake in creative AI adoption and the impacts practitioners report on their creative work. The study surfaces three dominant narrative types: generative AI as tool (instrumental), as collaborator (relational), and as threat (existential) — and documents how these narratives correlate with different value commitments and adoption strategies. The paper argues for a values-centered account of creative AI adoption.

## Key Concepts
- Creative professional AI narratives (tool / collaborator / threat)
- Values in creative AI adoption
- Generative AI impacts on creative practice
- Human-AI creative relationship types
- Creative identity and AI

## Theoretical Framework
Values in design (Friedman & Hendry); creative cognition; sociotechnical systems; qualitative HCI methodology; the paper draws on values-centered design and creative practice research traditions.

## Methods
Semi-structured interviews with 30+ creative professionals across multiple disciplines (visual art, music, writing, game design, graphic design); thematic analysis of narrative types and value structures.

## Main Arguments
- Creative professionals construct coherent narratives about AI that reflect their professional values and shape their adoption strategies
- The tool narrative treats AI as an accelerant for execution; the collaborator narrative treats it as a creative partner with its own aesthetic contributions; the threat narrative foregrounds concerns about livelihood and creative authenticity
- Practitioners' values (originality, craft, human connection, economic security) are the strongest predictors of which narrative they adopt
- Design of AI tools for creative professionals should be informed by the diversity of value commitments, not just productivity metrics

## Limitations & Critiques
The three-narrative typology may oversimplify a complex landscape; Microsoft Research institutional context may influence findings; the study captures a specific moment in creative AI adoption that may have shifted.

# The Application of Generative AI in Design-Based Elementary Education


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.32431/kace.2026.29.1.011](https://doi.org/10.32431/kace.2026.29.1.011)

## Summary
This paper examines the application of generative AI in design-based elementary education, investigating how young students can engage with AI as a design tool and what pedagogical frameworks support meaningful AI-integrated design learning at the K-6 level. The research documents teacher strategies, student engagement patterns, and learning outcomes when elementary students use age-appropriate AI design tools in project-based contexts. The paper argues that early AI design education can build both technological literacy and design thinking skills simultaneously.

## Key Concepts
- Generative AI in elementary/K-6 design education
- Design-based learning for young children
- AI literacy development in early education
- Age-appropriate AI design tools
- Teacher preparation for AI-integrated design instruction

## Theoretical Framework
Design-based learning; constructionist pedagogy (Papert); AI literacy frameworks; draws on child development and early childhood education technology research.

## Methods
Classroom-based research study; qualitative and quantitative data from elementary design courses using AI tools; teacher interviews and classroom observation; student work artifact analysis.

## Main Arguments
- Elementary students can engage meaningfully with AI design tools when appropriately scaffolded
- Design-based contexts provide authentic purposes for AI use that make learning more motivating and meaningful
- Early AI design education builds both technical AI literacy and transferable design thinking skills
- Teachers need specific professional development to facilitate AI-integrated design learning at the elementary level

## Limitations & Critiques
Limited to specific age groups and tool contexts; the rapid evolution of AI tools may quickly date specific findings; scale effects and equity implications of AI in elementary design education require further investigation.

# The Role of Large Language Models in UI/UX Design: A Systematic Review


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.5143/jesk.2024.43.6.575](https://doi.org/10.5143/jesk.2024.43.6.575)

## Summary
This systematic review examines the growing literature on the role of large language models (LLMs) in UI/UX design, cataloguing how LLMs are being used across the design process: from user research and requirements synthesis to wireframing support, design pattern generation, and usability evaluation. The review finds that LLMs show significant promise for automating routine design documentation and supporting ideation, but consistently struggle with tasks requiring aesthetic judgment, contextual user understanding, and iterative refinement based on design-specific feedback. The paper maps current capabilities and critical gaps for the research agenda.

## Key Concepts
- Large language models (LLMs) in UI/UX design
- Systematic review of AI design tools
- LLM capabilities and limitations in design tasks
- Design process automation and augmentation
- Research gaps in LLM-assisted design

## Theoretical Framework
Systematic review methodology; human-computer interaction; AI capabilities assessment; draws on design process models (double diamond, IDEO) to organize the review's taxonomy of AI applications.

## Methods
Systematic literature review; search across HCI, AI, and design research databases; thematic coding of LLM application types, evaluation methods, and findings; analysis of 40+ papers on LLMs in design contexts.

## Main Arguments
- LLMs are most effective in design contexts that involve text processing, documentation, and pattern matching from training data
- Creative, aesthetic, and empathic dimensions of UI/UX design remain challenging for LLMs in current forms
- The most promising applications combine LLM text capabilities with human designer judgment and iteration
- The field lacks standardized evaluation frameworks for assessing LLM-assisted design quality

## Limitations & Critiques
The rapid evolution of LLMs means the review may be partially outdated by publication; heterogeneous study designs make cross-study comparison difficult; the review does not address LLMs' impact on UX practitioner skill development.

# Instructional Message Design (Bishop)


## Abstract
Instructional message design explores how various media and delivery systems might be used more effectively to help optimize instructional communications within context-speci ﬁ c instructional situations and learner needs. But use of the term appears to have fallen out of favor over the years since the mid-1990s. A review of the historical and theoretical founda- tions of instructional message design reveals that, while instructional design generally has shifted from objectivist t

**DOI:** [10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_30](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_30)

## Summary
Bishop's chapter on instructional message design synthesizes principles for how visual and textual information should be organized and presented to support learning. Drawing on cognitive and perceptual psychology, the chapter covers principles of text layout, visual design, and multimedia integration that instructional designers use to reduce extraneous cognitive load and support meaningful processing. It serves as a practical reference bridging learning science and communication design in educational contexts.

## Key Concepts
- Instructional message design
- Cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer)
- Visual perception and attention principles
- Text-image integration
- Typography and layout for learning

## Theoretical Framework
Cognitive multimedia learning theory and instructional communication design; draws on dual-coding theory (Paivio), cognitive load theory, and Gestalt perceptual principles.

## Methods
Literature synthesis; handbook chapter drawing on experimental research in educational psychology and instructional design to produce design guidelines.

## Main Arguments
- The arrangement of text, images, and white space significantly affects learning by managing cognitive load
- Contiguity, coherence, and redundancy principles should guide multimedia design decisions
- Designers must account for both the information content and the cognitive architecture of the learner
- Poor message design creates unnecessary processing burdens that reduce learning effectiveness

## Limitations & Critiques
Much of the empirical foundation comes from controlled laboratory settings; real-world message design involves constraints (branding, accessibility, platform) that the principles do not fully address.

# Integrating AI into the Design Process


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.32403/0554-4866-2024-2-88-133-139](https://doi.org/10.32403/0554-4866-2024-2-88-133-139)

## Summary
This practitioner-oriented paper examines methods and frameworks for integrating AI into the design process across multiple design disciplines, offering a taxonomy of AI integration points and design process stages where AI adds most value. Drawing on case studies from product design, graphic design, and UX, the paper argues that AI integration is most effective when designed around the designer's process rather than around the AI tool's capabilities. The paper provides practical frameworks for designers seeking to systematically incorporate AI into professional practice.

## Key Concepts
- AI integration in design process
- Design process stage analysis (research, ideation, prototyping, production)
- AI as process augmentation vs. replacement
- Human oversight in AI-integrated design
- Taxonomy of AI design tools by function

## Theoretical Framework
Design process methodology; human-centered AI integration; draws on established design process models (double diamond, UCD) to organize AI integration strategy.

## Methods
Multiple case studies across design disciplines; practitioner documentation and reflection; taxonomy development from empirical cases; literature review of AI design tool capabilities.

## Main Arguments
- AI integration works best when it augments specific, bounded phases of the design process rather than being applied uniformly across all design work
- Designers who understand their own process can identify the highest-value AI integration points; those who don't tend toward superficial AI use
- Human oversight and editorial judgment remain essential at all stages of AI-integrated design work
- The taxonomy of AI tools by design function helps designers match tools to process needs rather than adopting tools opportunistically

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study evidence is primarily from design disciplines with strong visual output; service design and systems design integration is less thoroughly addressed; the pace of AI tool development means specific tool recommendations will date quickly.

# Exploring the Impact of AI Language Model ChatGPT on User Experience (IJTIM)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.54489/ijtim.v3i1.195](https://doi.org/10.54489/ijtim.v3i1.195)

This study investigates the integration of AI language model tools, specifically ChatGPT, in the Design Thinking process to evaluate their effect on product design. While previous research has primarily focused on Design Thinking, limited research has been conducted on the application of AI tools in the process. This study involved redesigning two previous projects using AI tools in the Design Thinking process. We conducted interviews with five designers and analysed ten Product Manager reports to understand the impact of using AI tools on one of the most popular innovation and problem-solving approaches called Design Thinking. The findings indicate that integrating AI tools into the design thinking process, specifically in the Define and Ideate stages, can improve the efficiency and creativity of the UI. However, the successful implementation of AI tools requires a combination of technological expertise and creative design thinking. The study emphasizes the potential for AI tools to complement human creativity and expertise in the design process, rather than replace them. The results contribute to understanding the appropriate application of AI tools in design and innovation while underscoring the importance of keeping humans at the centre of the process.

## Summary
This paper examines the impact of ChatGPT on user experience design work, investigating how UX practitioners are incorporating the large language model into research, writing, and prototyping tasks. Through a survey and interview study with UX practitioners, the authors document how ChatGPT is being used to generate interview questions, synthesize research notes, draft UX writing, and explain design rationale — while identifying the accuracy, hallucination, and generic output problems practitioners encounter. The paper provides a practical assessment of ChatGPT's current utility and limitations for UX work.

## Key Concepts
- ChatGPT in UX research and design workflows
- AI hallucination and accuracy concerns in UX
- UX writing and AI text generation
- AI for design documentation and rationale
- Practitioner AI adoption in UX

## Theoretical Framework
Technology assessment; human-AI collaboration in professional practice; UX practice research; draws on technology adoption and practitioner-AI collaboration literature.

## Methods
Mixed-methods study; online survey with UX practitioners; follow-up qualitative interviews; analysis of ChatGPT use patterns, perceived utility, and experienced limitations.

## Main Arguments
- UX practitioners are adopting ChatGPT rapidly for text-heavy tasks (documentation, question generation, synthesizing notes) where it provides genuine time savings
- Hallucination and generic output are the most significant practical concerns, requiring practitioners to develop verification habits
- ChatGPT is least useful for tasks requiring deep contextual knowledge of specific users, organizations, or projects
- Effective ChatGPT integration requires practitioners to develop prompt literacy and output verification skills as new professional competencies
