# Design Research Society Design Research Society

## Summary
Schneider and Csűrös (Moholy-Nagy University of Art and Design Budapest / Future Potentials Observatory) theorize generative AI's role in design through the lens of design philosophy and the "material turn" in design theory. They argue that GenAI constitutes a new kind of distributed creative agency that challenges established notions of authorship, intentionality, and material resistance in design. Drawing on posthumanist and new materialist frameworks, the paper positions GenAI not as a tool but as an active participant in distributed creativity—co-shaping design outcomes through its own "generative logic."

## Key Concepts
- **Distributed creativity**: Creativity understood as distributed across human designers, materials, tools, and context rather than residing in individual human genius
- **Material turn in design**: Theoretical move emphasizing the active role of materials and technologies in shaping design processes and outcomes
- **Generative logic**: GenAI's internal tendencies (learned distributions, latent spaces) that actively shape outputs beyond designer intent
- **Posthumanist design**: Design theory that decenters the human designer as sole creative agent
- **Authorship dissolution**: The challenge GenAI poses to traditional conceptions of creative ownership and intentional design

## Theoretical Framework
Posthumanist and new materialist philosophy (Barad, Latour, Ingold) applied to design theory. The "material turn" frames design materials—including AI—as having affordances and resistances that actively participate in shaping design outcomes.

## Methods
Conceptual/theoretical analysis presented at EKSIG 2025 (Design Research Society Experiential Knowledge conference). No empirical data; philosophical argument and design theory synthesis.

## Main Arguments
1. GenAI is not a neutral tool but an active participant in design with its own generative logic shaped by training data and model architecture
2. Distributed creativity frameworks better account for human-GenAI design practice than tool-use or authorship models
3. The material turn's insights—that materials resist and redirect designer intent—apply to GenAI: its latent spaces and learned biases push back against designer intentions
4. Design philosophy must evolve to account for AI as a creative agent without collapsing into either AI determinism or naive tool instrumentalism

## Limitations
Highly theoretical paper that may be difficult to translate into practical design education or practice guidance. Posthumanist frameworks are contested and not universally accepted in design research. Conference paper format limits depth of argument.

## Connections
- Connects to [[Ethical Dimensions of AI in Graphic Design]] on AI's challenge to design authorship and authenticity
- Relates to [[Poets Over Quants Automation Increases Value of Creativity]] on how automation changes creative value
- Pairs with [[The Impact of AI Development on the Future of Work]] on AI's redefinition of designer roles

# Designerly Ways of Knowing (Cross 1982)

**DOI:** [10.5040/9781474282932.0018](https://doi.org/10.5040/9781474282932.0018)

## Summary
Cross's foundational 1982 paper argues that design constitutes a genuine "third culture" of human knowledge alongside the sciences and the humanities — each with its own phenomenon of study, appropriate methods, and core values. Design's phenomenon is the man-made world; its methods are modelling, pattern-formation, and synthesis; its values center on practicality, ingenuity, empathy, and appropriateness. Cross argues that this third culture has been neglected and needs to be articulated as a legitimate basis for design research and education, with intrinsic rather than merely instrumental aims.

## Key Concepts
- Third culture (design alongside sciences and humanities)
- Designerly ways of knowing
- Modelling and synthesis as core design methods
- Appropriateness as design's central value
- Design as a distinct academic discipline

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on Bruce Archer's RCA research project on "Design in general education"; contrasts design epistemology with scientific (experiment, classification, analysis) and humanistic (analogy, metaphor, criticism) modes of inquiry.

## Methods
Theoretical/conceptual paper; comparative analysis of knowledge structures across disciplines; draws on the Royal College of Art project findings and broader educational philosophy.

## Main Arguments
- Design is not applied science or applied humanities; it has its own genuinely distinct ways of knowing that deserve recognition as a third area of education
- The "language" of design is modelling — the ability to construct, test, and communicate through representations of the not-yet-existing
- Design education oriented solely toward instrumental skill development misses the intrinsic values of the designerly tradition
- Recognizing design as a third culture has implications for both research (what counts as design knowledge?) and education (what should design students learn?)

## Limitations
- Written in 1982; some disciplinary assumptions have been complicated by design's subsequent diversification and institutionalization in computing, HCI, and service design
- "Third culture" framing may oversimplify the overlaps and tensions between design and scientific/humanistic inquiry

## Connections
Foundational for [[Educating for Design Character (Boling Gray Smith)]] and [[Conceptions of Design Practice (Lotsos et al. Northwestern)]]; relates to [[Anatomy of Prototypes (Lim Stolterman Tenenberg)]] on design knowledge; informs [[Developing Human Experience Experts (Cheatham Miami U)]] on design epistemology.

# Designing Job Characteristics for Hybrid Intelligence (Yang and Jiang)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1108/pr-03-2024-0229](https://doi.org/10.1108/pr-03-2024-0229)
PurposeThe fusion of human intelligence with artificial intelligence is a promising approach for addressing complex challenges, giving rise to the concept of hybrid intelligence. However, principles for guiding the design and management of hybrid intelligence are lacking. This study addresses this gap by exploring the key characteristics of job positions necessary for effective hybrid intelligence. Drawing upon the job characteristic theory (JCT), we identify key job features relevant to hybrid intelligence work, elucidating the challenges and considerations inherent in this domain.Design/methodology/approachThe study conducted 23 semi-structured interviews with middle-level managers from ten service companies in China, exploring their experiences with human–AI collaboration within their organisations. The analysis employed both inductive and deductive methods. Inductive coding was used to identify emerging themes from the participants’ responses, while the deductive approach ensured that these themes aligned with the research questions and Hackman and Oldham’s JCT.FindingsThe results contribute to our understanding of the job positions required for successful hybrid intelligence implementation, offering both theoretical and practical perspectives on job design and JCT applications in the era of intelligent technologies.Originality/valueOur findings illuminate the critical job characteristics essential for integrating hybrid intelligence into organisational systems, highlighting the evolution of job roles and the implications for effective job design in the intelligent era. These insights inform the ongoing discourse on job design and adaptation in the face of rapidly evolving technological advancements, guiding organisations seeking to harness the full potential of hybrid intelligence.

## Summary
Yang and Jiang apply Hackman and Oldham's Job Characteristics Theory (JCT) to the emerging context of hybrid intelligence — human-AI collaboration in organizational work — asking what job characteristics enable effective integration of AI into workers' roles. Drawing on 23 semi-structured interviews with middle managers in Chinese service companies, they identify how JCT dimensions (skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, feedback) are reconfigured in hybrid intelligence contexts, offering both theoretical extensions of JCT and practical principles for job design in AI-integrated organizations.

## Key Concepts
- Hybrid intelligence (human-AI collaboration)
- Job Characteristics Theory (Hackman and Oldham 1975)
- Skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, feedback
- Job design for AI-integrated work
- Human-AI task allocation

## Theoretical Framework
Extends Hackman and Oldham's JCT to hybrid intelligence; uses both inductive (emergent themes from interviews) and deductive (JCT framework) coding; frames effective hybrid intelligence as a job design challenge, not merely a technology implementation challenge.

## Methods
Qualitative; 23 semi-structured interviews with middle-level managers

# Designing the Constraints: Co-creation Exercises (Eckert and Stacey)

## Summary
Eckert and Stacey analyze a co-creation exercise conducted by a European car company's UX team with Chinese consumers, aimed at eliciting consumer values to inform product and service design for the Chinese market. They compare this value elicitation approach to the "constraint gathering" phase in artistic design processes — specifically fashion and knitwear — where designers use inspiration and mood boards to frame the space of acceptable designs. The paper argues that co-creation exercises play an analogous role to artistic sources of inspiration, framing design possibilities through consumer-voiced values.

## Key Concepts
- Co-creation exercises for value elicitation
- Design constraints as framing mechanism
- Consumer values and design space definition
- Cross-cultural design research
- Mood boards and constraint sets in design

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on design cognition research and Eckert and Stacey's prior work on design constraints; relates user research to design framing; uses fashion/knitwear design as an analogical lens for interpreting the car company's consumer research process.

## Methods
Qualitative case analysis; analysis of datasets from co-creation workshops between European UX team and Chinese consumer groups; comparative analysis with artistic design constraint-gathering processes; conceptual synthesis.

## Main Arguments
- Co-creation exercises do not produce direct design specifications but rather frame the design space — they define what kinds of solutions are acceptable by articulating consumer values
- This framing function is analogous to how artistic designers use inspiration sources and constraints to bound the design space before generative work begins
- Cross-cultural design research must account for the fact that consumers articulate values through cultural reference frames that designers may not share — the co-creation process must create mutual intelligibility
- Mood boards and narrative-based value elicitation are complementary, not competing — one produces constraint sets, the other produces cultural meaning that designers must interpret into constraints

## Limitations
- Case study of a single European-Chinese design collaboration; cultural dynamics and power asymmetries in other cross-cultural design research may differ significantly
- The "co-creation" exercise analyzed was not truly co-creative in the collaborative sense — consumers and designers did not jointly create; consumers created and designers observed

UdeM)]] on authentic co-design practices.

# Developing Human Experience Experts (Cheatham Miami U)

**DOI:** [10.1007/978-3-031-93233-5_3](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-93233-5_3)

## Summary
Cheatham's work examines how design education programs can develop what she terms "Human Experience (HX) experts" — designers who integrate deep technical competence with empathic, human-centered sensibility and ethical awareness. The paper argues that HX expertise requires pedagogical models that go beyond skill-based training to cultivate reflective practitioners capable of navigating complex sociotechnical contexts. Curricular design implications are drawn for programs preparing the next generation of designers and UX professionals.

## Key Concepts
- Human Experience (HX) expertise
- Empathic design competence
- Reflective practitioner (Schön)
- Sociotechnical competency
- Design curriculum design

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on Schön's reflective practitioner model, Dreyfus skill acquisition stages, and human-centered design philosophy; positions HX expertise as a holistic developmental trajectory rather than a set of discrete skills.

## Methods
Curricular analysis and conceptual framework development; draws on program design experiences and student learning outcome data at Miami University's design programs.

## Main Arguments
- Traditional design education emphasizes artifact production and tool mastery at the expense of developing practitioners' capacity to reason about human experience in context
- HX expertise requires integrating emotional intelligence, systems thinking, and ethical reasoning alongside technical craft
- Studio pedagogy must create authentic, reflective experiences — not just project delivery — to develop this fuller professional capacity
- Industry partnerships and real-world complexity are essential to developing HX expertise at appropriate levels of challenge

## Limitations
- Framework is institution-specific and may require adaptation across different program sizes, resources, and student populations
- Assessment of holistic HX expertise development remains methodologically challenging

## Connections
Relates to [[Educating for Design Character (Boling Gray Smith)]] on character-centered pedagogy; connects to [[Conceptions of Design Practice (Lotsos et al. # Do Artifacts Have Politics? (Winner 1980)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.4324/9781315259697-21](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315259697-21)
In controversies about technology and society, there is no idea more pro vocative than the notion that technical things have political qualities. At issue is the claim that the machines, structures, and systems of modern material culture can be accurately judged not only for their contributions of efficiency and pro ductivity, not merely for their positive and negative environmental side effects, but also for the ways in which they can embody specific forms of power and authority. Since ideas of this kind have a persistent and troubling presence in discussions about the meaning of technology, they deserve explicit attention.1 Writing in Technology and Culture almost two decades ago, Lewis Mumford gave classic statement to one version of the theme, arguing that "from late neo lithic times in the Near East, right down to our own day, two technologies have recurrently existed side by side: one authoritarian, the other democratic, the first system-centered, immensely powerful, but inherently unstable, the other man-centered, relatively weak, but resourceful and durable."2 This thesis stands at the heart of Mumford's studies of the city, architecture, and the his tory of technics, and mirrors concerns voiced earlier in the works of Peter Kropotkin, William Morris, and other nineteenth century critics of industrial ism. More recently, antinuclear and prosolar energy movements in Europe and America have adopted a similar notion as a centerpiece in their arguments. Thus environmentalist Denis Hayes concludes, "The increased deployment of nuclear power facilities must lead society toward authoritarianism. Indeed, safe reliance upon nuclear power as the principal source of energy may be possible only in a totalitarian state." Echoing the views of many proponents of appropri ate technology and the soft energy path, Hayes contends that "dispersed solar sources are more compatible than centralized technologies with social equity, freedom and cultural pluralism."3 An eagerness to interpret technical artifacts in political language is by no means the exclusive property of critics of large-scale high-technology systems. A long lineage of boosters have insisted that the "biggest and best" that science and industry made available were the best guarantees of democracy, freedom, and social justice. The factory system, automobile, telephone, radio, television, the space program, and of course nuclear power itself have all at one time or another been described as democratizing, liberating forces. David Lilienthal, in T.V.A.: Democracy on the March, for example, found this promise in the phos 121

## Summary
Winner's landmark 1980 essay argues that technical artifacts — bridges, buildings, machines, systems — can embody and enact specific political properties, not merely reflect the social or economic systems around them. He distinguishes two ways artifacts have politics: (1) as a consequence of deliberate design choices that favor certain social arrangements (e.g., Robert Moses's low-clearance Long Island bridges, allegedly designed to exclude buses and thereby Black beachgoers)

# Does AI Development Polarized Job Market:

## Summary
Hamadou et al. (2025, preprint, Universitas Islam International Indonesia) examine whether AI development polarizes labor markets using dynamic panel analysis across multiple countries from 2000–2022. Using Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) techniques on macroeconomic panel data, the study finds mixed evidence: AI-driven automation displaces certain routine and semi-routine labor categories, but also creates new employment opportunities in sectors with intensive technological adoption. A job market polarization pattern—growth in high-skill and low-skill jobs with hollowing of middle-skill employment—is confirmed for most economies studied.

## Key Concepts
- **Job market polarization**: Automation disproportionately displaces middle-skill routine jobs while high-skill and low-skill work persists
- **GMM (Generalized Method of Moments)**: Dynamic panel estimation that addresses endogeneity and heterogeneity in panel data
- **Task-biased technological change**: AI substitutes for routine cognitive and manual tasks, complementing non-routine tasks
- **Sector-specific displacement effects**: AI's labor market impacts vary significantly across industries

## Theoretical Framework
Built on task-biased technological change theory (Autor, Levy, Murnane) and Acemoglu's framework on automation and labor market polarization. Dynamic panel methods capture both short- and long-run displacement effects across economies.

## Methods
Quantitative, using panel data from 2000–2022 across multiple economies. GMM estimation with AI penetration indices as key independent variables; unemployment and employment composition as outcomes. Pre-print; peer review pending.

## Main Arguments
1. AI development exhibits a statistically significant job displacement effect on routine and semi-routine occupations
2. New employment opportunities emerge in high-technology sectors, partially offsetting displacement
3. The polarization effect is more pronounced in economies with weaker labor market protections
4. Macro-level panel evidence confirms task-biased technological change predictions at national scale

## Limitations
Pre-print; not peer reviewed. Measurement of "AI development" at macro level is imprecise—proxied by patents or R&D investment rather than direct AI deployment measures. GMM estimates are sensitive to instrument selection. Cross-national analysis may obscure important institutional variation.

# E1C01_1 10/14/2009 5

## Summary
Wilmoth, Prigmore, and Bray provide an overview of the major models in the Human Performance Technology (HPT) field, tracing their conceptual foundations and practical applications. The chapter surveys foundational HPT models including Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model, Rummler and Brache's performance system model, and the ISPI HPT model, examining how each conceptualizes the relationship between human performance, environmental factors, and organizational systems. The authors argue that HPT models share a commitment to systematic analysis, cause diagnosis, and evidence-based intervention selection that distinguishes HPT from ad hoc training approaches.

## Key Concepts
- **Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model (BEM)**: Framework distinguishing environmental supports (information, resources, incentives) from individual repertoire (knowledge, capacity, motivation) as causes of performance gaps
- **Rummler-Brache Performance System Model**: Three-level model (organization, process, job/performer) for understanding performance in context
- **ISPI HPT Model**: The International Society for Performance Improvement's comprehensive process model for performance improvement
- **Performance analysis**: The diagnostic process of identifying gaps between actual and desired performance
- **Systematic intervention selection**: Matching solutions to diagnosed causes rather than defaulting to training

## Theoretical Framework
Behavioral and systems theory foundations; HPT models integrate behavioral psychology (Skinner, Gilbert), systems engineering, and organizational development. The shared commitment is to empirical analysis rather than theoretical advocacy.

## Methods
Literature review and conceptual synthesis of major HPT models; practitioner-oriented analysis of each model's structure, assumptions, and application domains.

## Main Arguments
1. HPT models share a commitment to systematic diagnosis before intervention—the field-defining move that distinguishes HPT from training-first approaches
2. Gilbert's BEM remains the most influential diagnostic framework because it directs attention away from individual deficit toward environmental causes
3. Rummler-Brache contributes the insight that performance problems are often process and system problems, not individual performance problems
4. The proliferation of HPT models reflects the field's maturation and the diversity of contexts in which performance improvement is practiced

## Limitations
The overview necessarily simplifies models that have substantial complexity in full application. The field has continued to evolve since publication; more recent frameworks integrating technology, learning analytics, and AI are not covered.

- Pairs with [[The Current State of Human]] (Cho et al.) on HPT's intellectual structure through citation analysis

# Educating for Design Character (Boling Gray Smith)

**DOI:** [10.21606/drs.2020.120](https://doi.org/10.21606/drs.2020.120)

## Summary
Boling, Gray, and Smith argue that design pedagogy must shift from a primarily cognitive focus — skills, knowledge, design moves — to cultivating "design character": the full dispositional orientation of the designer, including beliefs, values, experiential knowledge, and judgment. Drawing on 20+ years of combined studio teaching across Indiana University and Purdue, they use a co/autoethnographic approach to surface pedagogical challenges organized around students, curriculum, colleagues, and self. The paper positions character as foundational to the future of design practice.

## Key Concepts
- Design character (Nelson and Stolterman's philosophical perspective)
- Studio pedagogy
- Co/autoethnographic method
- Design disposition vs. design cognition
- Character-centered design education

## Theoretical Framework
Grounds in Nelson and Stolterman's (2012) philosophical account of design; explicitly contrasts with the dominant cognitive perspective (Cross, Lawson, Schön); frames character as the holistic integration of being-in-the-world, not just expert thinking.

## Methods
Co/autoethnographic reflection by three studio educators (Boling, Gray, Smith) across three design disciplines and multiple curricular levels; review of embedded studies conducted during studio teaching; extended mutual discussion and analysis.

## Main Arguments
- Teaching for design character creates pedagogical challenges distinct from skills-based or cognitive approaches: it requires attending to students' whole person, values formation, and long-term growth trajectories
- Curricular challenges include assessing character development without reducing it to observable behaviors; colleague challenges include working with co-instructors who hold different pedagogical philosophies
- The "self" challenge for educators is significant: teaching from character requires modeling character, demanding personal reflection and sustained commitment
- Without character formation, design education produces technically capable practitioners who may lack the ethical grounding and judgment for the work's real demands

## Limitations
- Autoethnographic method is inherently perspective-bound; findings reflect these three educators' specific institutional and disciplinary contexts
- "Design character" is philosophically rich but operationally under-specified, making it difficult to assess or systematically cultivate

## Connections
Directly links to [[Conceptions of Design Practice (Lotsos et al. Northwestern)]] on designer identity; relates to [[Developing Human Experience Experts (Cheatham Miami U)]] on holistic professional development; informs [[Designerly Ways of Knowing (Cross 1982)]] on foundational design epistemology.

# EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST,42(2), 99–107

## Summary
Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, and Chinn (2007) respond to Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark's (2006) argument that minimally guided instruction is ineffective. The authors demonstrate that Kirschner et al. mischaracterize problem-based learning (PBL) and inquiry learning (IL) as "minimally guided" when in fact both approaches are highly scaffolded. Drawing on empirical evidence, Hmelo-Silver et al. argue that PBL and IL produce deep learning, transfer, and professional competencies that direct instruction cannot match, precisely because they structure guided inquiry rather than abandoning guidance.

## Key Concepts
- **Scaffolding in PBL/IL**: Structural supports including problem design, facilitator guidance, structured debriefing, and collaborative protocols that distinguish PBL/IL from unguided discovery
- **Mischaracterization of PBL**: Kirschner et al. conflate PBL and IL with pure discovery learning; Hmelo-Silver et al. show these are empirically distinct approaches
- **Transfer evidence**: PBL graduates demonstrate superior transfer of learning to novel clinical and professional contexts compared to conventionally instructed peers
- **Cognitive load in PBL**: Well-designed PBL manages cognitive load through scaffolding, not by eliminating it through direct instruction
- **Knowledge in use**: PBL develops integrated, applicable knowledge rather than inert knowledge acquired through direct instruction

## Theoretical Framework
Constructivist and situated learning theories; draws on empirical research from medical, science, and professional education. Argues that scaffolded inquiry is consistent with—not contrary to—cognitive learning principles.

## Methods
Systematic review and synthesis of empirical research on PBL and inquiry learning outcomes; meta-analyses and longitudinal studies from medical education and science education.

## Main Arguments
1. PBL and IL are not minimally guided—they employ extensive scaffolding that addresses cognitive load concerns
2. Kirschner et al.'s critique applies to pure discovery learning, not to the scaffolded inquiry of PBL and IL
3. Empirical evidence consistently shows PBL and IL produce strong transfer and professional competency outcomes
4. The debate is not "guidance vs. no guidance" but "what kinds of guidance best support complex learning"

## Limitations
Most PBL evidence comes from medical education; generalizability to other disciplines is sometimes contested. Long-term outcomes are more favorable than short-term knowledge acquisition—which may disadvantage PBL in contexts emphasizing exam performance.

## Connections
- Directly responds to [[KIRSCHNER, SWELLER, CLARKMINIMAL GUIDANCE]] on the guided vs. minimal guidance debate
- Connects to [[Problem-Based Learning]] on PBL's theoretical foundations and methods
- Relates to [[Scaffolding and Achievement in Problem-Based and Inquiry Learning]] (same paper, different note)

# Embracing the AI/automation age:

## Summary
Tenakwah and Watson (Charles Darwin University, Australia) present a conceptual framework for preparing workforces for the AI and automation age, emphasizing strategic human resource management and leadership. Through integrative literature review and industry expert insights, they identify strategic workforce planning, AI literacy development, new AI-centric role creation, and reskilling as essential organizational responses. The paper argues that successfully navigating AI integration requires proactive HR leadership that treats AI not as a replacement threat but as a catalyst for human-AI collaboration.

## Key Concepts
- **Strategic workforce planning**: Aligning AI/automation strategies with long-term business goals
- **AI literacy**: Workforce capability to understand, use, and adapt alongside AI systems
- **Human-AI collaboration**: Rethinking work design so humans and machines complement each other
- **New AI-centric roles**: Emerging job categories (AI trainers, ethics monitors) requiring human judgment
- **Reskilling and upskilling**: Continuous learning programs enabling workers to adapt to AI-transformed roles

## Theoretical Framework
Conceptual, drawing on strategic HRM theory, organizational learning, and human-AI teaming literature. Synthesizes existing research into prescriptive guidance for HR practitioners, bridging macro workforce trends with organizational design decisions.

## Methods
Conceptual paper with integrative literature review. Draws on published research, industry reports, and practitioner case examples. No primary data collection; framework development is the contribution.

## Main Arguments
1. Organizations that treat AI as purely a productivity tool miss the strategic opportunity to redesign work for human-AI complementarity
2. HR leadership must proactively anticipate skill gaps rather than reactively retrain after displacement occurs
3. AI literacy must be embedded throughout the organization, not just in technical teams
4. Cultural readiness (psychological safety, growth mindset) is as important as technical training

## Limitations
Conceptual framework without empirical validation; cross-sector generalizations may not hold across industries with varying AI maturity. Australian organizational context may limit direct applicability elsewhere.

## Connections
- Complements [[Fr om code to collaboration]] on AI's impact on IT workforce dynamics
- Relates to [[Unlocking training transfer in the age of]] on training transfer in AI-transformed workplaces
- Connects to [[Does AI Development Polarized Job Market]] on macro-level labor market effects

# Employment Shopping: An AI-Driven Universal Job Allocation Model for Inclusive

## Summary
This paper proposes "Employment Shopping," an AI-powered mobile employment solution designed to address workforce exclusion for marginalized groups — ex-offenders, rural workers, and people with disabilities. Grounded in labor market segmentation theory and critique of institutional barriers, the paper argues that existing AI-driven job platforms reproduce systemic exclusion through digital access gaps and algorithmic bias. The proposed model combines personalized AI job recommendations with in-person support via mobile Employment Buses, functioning as institutional entrepreneurship using bias-mitigating AI and public-private partnerships.

## Key Concepts
- AI-driven job matching and recommendation systems
- Labor market segmentation theory
- Algorithmic bias in employment platforms
- Institutional entrepreneurship
- Mobile social infrastructure (Employment Buses)

## Theoretical Framework
Grounded in labor market segmentation theory (dual labor market, institutional barriers) and institutional entrepreneurship literature; critiques AI systems that optimize within existing market structures, reproducing exclusion; frames Employment Shopping as a socio-technical intervention that redesigns the infrastructure of labor market access.

## Methods
Conceptual/design proposal paper; theoretical grounding in labor market and institutional theory; feasibility and ethical analysis; alignment with UN SDG frameworks on poverty reduction, decent work, and reduced inequalities.

## Main Arguments
- Existing AI-driven employment platforms are built for users with digital access, stable addresses, and standard employment histories — systematically excluding the most marginalized job seekers
- Algorithmic bias in job matching reflects and amplifies historical discrimination; bias mitigation requires deliberate technical and governance interventions, not neutral optimization
- Mobile Employment Buses address the physical infrastructure gap: bringing AI-assisted job matching to communities without stable internet access or proximity to employment centers
- Public-private partnership models can enable scalable, sustainable deployment without relying exclusively on government resources

## Limitations
- Conceptual proposal without empirical implementation; feasibility is argued but not demonstrated
- Bias-mitigating AI is presented as achievable without specifying which specific bias mitigation approaches would be used or how they would be evaluated

## Connections
Relates to [[AI Impact on Diversity and Job Displacement in ICT (Brown dissertation)]] on AI and workforce equity; links to [[Co-Producing AI Augmented Participatory Lifecycle (Mushkani et al. UdeM)]] on inclusive AI development; connects to [[Rethinking Optimization Systems-Based Social Externalities (Nokhiz et al. Cornel.md)]] on addressing AI optimization's exclusionary effects.

# Ensmenger - The Rise of Computer Science

## Summary
Ensmenger's chapter traces the disciplinary formation of computer science from the late 1940s–1960s, when programming was done primarily by female "human computers" and clerical workers, through its transformation into a credentialed, predominantly male academic discipline. The chapter reveals how professionalization of CS involved deliberate boundary work—constructing aptitude tests, establishing degree programs, and cultivating a "programmer personality" stereotype—that systematically excluded women and working-class practitioners who had built computing from the ground up.

## Key Concepts
- **"Human computers"**: Female mathematicians who performed manual computation before electronic computers and transitioned into programming
- **Aptitude testing**: Psychometric tests used to certify programmer identity and professionalize access to the field
- **Boundary work**: Social processes by which occupations define who counts as a legitimate practitioner
- **Professionalization**: Transformation of programming from an open, heterogeneous practice into a credentialed discipline
- **The "programmer personality"**: A cultural construction emphasizing mathematical aptitude and antisocial traits

## Theoretical Framework
Science and Technology Studies (STS) / sociology of knowledge. Draws on sociology of professions (Abbott) and historical analysis of how disciplinary identities are constructed through social and institutional processes.

## Methods
Historical analysis using primary sources: memoirs, professional society documents, aptitude test archives, employer surveys, and trade publications from the 1940s–1970s.

## Main Arguments
1. Computing's early practitioners were diverse—including many women—but disciplinary formation systematically marginalized them
2. Aptitude testing was not a neutral meritocratic tool but a social instrument encoding particular cultural assumptions about who could be a programmer
3. The "gaming" and "puzzle-solving" culture of academic CS was constructed, not discovered as inherent to the work
4. The structure of CS as a discipline reflects its specific historical circumstances, not the essential nature of computation

## Limitations
Focus on U.S. context; international computing history may show different patterns. Emphasis on exclusionary dynamics may underweight genuine technical contributions of CS as a discipline.

## Connections
- Relates to [[How to Be Universal Some Cybernetic Strategies, 1943-70]] on the formation of adjacent computational disciplines
- Connects to broader STS frameworks in [[Orlikowski - Using Technology and Constituting Structures]]
- Situates historical context for contemporary debates on AI bias and representation

# Epistemic Insights AI Ethics via Constructionism (Lin and Dai CUHK)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1609/aaai.v39i28.35190](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v39i28.35190)
There is a growing consensus on the importance of AI ethics in K-12 education, yet effective teaching remains a challenge. AI ethics requires an interdisciplinary understanding of computer science, philosophy, and the humanities, alongside epistemic insights into how AI systems acquire, process, and apply knowledge differently from humans. To address this challenge, this study presents the design, development, and implementation of three theory-informed activities aimed at fostering epistemic insight and ethical understanding of AI among upper primary school students (ages 10-12). Grounded in constructionism, our pedagogical design leverages hands-on experimentation with guided reflection to concretize complex AI concepts. Students examine rule-based, data-driven, and generative AI systems, employing mathematical reasoning to represent AI decision-making processes and reflect on ethical issues such as fairness, bias, and transparency. The interdisciplinary, constructionist approach encourages learners to discern how AI knowledge construction differs from human cognition, thereby enhancing their ethical reasoning. The findings show that students not only developed a foundational understanding of ethical principles but also gained epistemic insight into AI’s relationship with human knowledge and values. This article provides a practical, theory-informed framework and interdisciplinary teaching resources to advance K-12 AI ethics education and support educators in fostering AI literacy.

## Summary
Lin and Dai present a constructionist pedagogical approach for developing epistemic insights into AI ethics among upper primary students (ages 10-12). They design three theory-informed activities in which students build and interact with rule-based, ML-based, and generative AI systems, using mathematical reasoning to represent AI decision-making and reflect on fairness, bias, and transparency. Findings show students developed not only foundational ethical principles but also genuine epistemic insight — understanding how AI knowledge construction differs from human cognition.

- Constructionist pedagogy (Papert)
- Epistemic insights into AI (how AI acquires/processes knowledge)
- K-12 AI ethics education

- Fairness, bias, and transparency as ethical concepts

Grounded in constructionism (learning by making) combined with an interdisciplinary approach spanning computer science, mathematics, philosophy, and humanities; distinguishes between AI literacy (broad) and epistemic insight (specific understanding of how AI differs from human knowing).

## Methods
Design-based curriculum development and implementation with upper primary students (AAAI 2025); three hands-on activities with guided reflection; qualitative analysis of student reasoning and artifacts.

# Ethical Dimensions of AI in Graphic Design

## Summary
Dedijer et al. (University of Novi Sad, Serbia) conduct a systematic literature review examining ethical challenges and opportunities of AI integration in graphic design practice. The paper analyzes authorship and originality, algorithmic bias in visual generation, transparency of training data sources, intellectual property, and displacement of human designers. While acknowledging AI's creative capabilities, the authors argue that ethical graphic design practice requires robust frameworks for accountability, transparency, and human oversight.

## Key Concepts
- **Authorship ambiguity**: Questions about creative agency when AI generates or heavily assists design work
- **Algorithmic bias in visual AI**: Training data biases manifest as aesthetic and representational stereotypes in generated outputs
- **Intellectual property**: Unresolved legal and ethical questions about AI's use of copyrighted training data and ownership of AI-generated work
- **Transparency**: Obligation to disclose when AI tools are used in creative production
- **Human designer's evolving role**: Shift from executor to curator, director, and ethical steward of AI outputs

## Theoretical Framework
Systematic literature review with an ethics-of-technology framing. Draws on established AI ethics frameworks (fairness, accountability, transparency) applied to the specific context of creative professional practice.

## Methods
Systematic literature review across multiple databases. Synthesizes empirical studies, theoretical papers, and practitioner accounts on AI in graphic design.

## Main Arguments
1. AI does not eliminate the need for human design judgment—it relocates it to curation, direction, and ethical oversight
2. Intellectual property frameworks are inadequate for AI-generated design work; significant legal ambiguity remains
3. Algorithmic bias produces visual outputs that perpetuate and amplify cultural stereotypes in training data
4. The graphic design community needs professional standards specific to AI-assisted work
5. AI's efficiency gains must be weighed against displacement risks and devaluation of human creative labor

## Limitations
Literature review rather than empirical study. The field moves faster than academic review cycles. Focus on graphic design may not generalize to all creative disciplines.

- Pairs with [[Design Research Society Design Research Society]] on AI in design philosophy

# EVALUATING

## Summary
Kirkpatrick's *Evaluating Training Programs: The Four Levels* presents the foundational framework for evaluating workplace training effectiveness across four levels: (1) Reaction—participant satisfaction; (2) Learning—knowledge and skill acquisition; (3) Behavior—on-the-job transfer; (4) Results—organizational outcomes. The book advocates moving beyond Level 1 (smile sheets) to demonstrate training's business value. The excerpted chapter covers reasons for evaluation: establishing credibility, justifying investment, and demonstrating value to organizational stakeholders.

## Key Concepts
- **Level 1 (Reaction)**: Participant satisfaction ratings collected immediately after training
- **Level 2 (Learning)**: Pre/post knowledge and skill assessment
- **Level 3 (Behavior)**: Observation or supervisor ratings of on-the-job behavior change after training
- **Level 4 (Results)**: Organizational metrics (productivity, quality, costs, turnover) attributed to training
- **Training credibility**: The organizational case for training as a value-adding function

## Theoretical Framework
Practical evaluation framework developed from Kirkpatrick's doctoral research and decades of training practice. Not grounded in a specific learning theory but in organizational pragmatics—demonstrating that training produces measurable organizational value.

## Methods
Prescriptive framework; based on practitioner experience and case illustrations rather than controlled research. Each level is described with practical guidance for data collection and use.

## Main Arguments
1. Training evaluation is essential for establishing and maintaining organizational credibility for L&D functions
2. Most organizations evaluate only at Level 1 (reaction), missing the most important evidence about effectiveness
3. Moving to Level 4 (results) requires patience, rigor, and collaboration with business stakeholders to isolate training's contribution
4. The four levels are hierarchically related: positive reactions do not guarantee learning; learning does not guarantee behavior change

## Limitations
Extensively criticized for conflating evaluation levels with causal relationships; positive correlations across levels do not establish that training caused the outcomes. Level 4 evaluation is notoriously difficult to attribute to training specifically amid other organizational influences.

- Extended and critiqued by [[Kirkpatrick Plus Evaluation and Continuous]]
- Relates to [[A Comparative Analysis]] (Fitzpatrick's comparative evaluation approaches)
- Connects to [[Program Evaluation]] on broader frameworks for program evaluation

# Evolving Roles of Creative Practitioners in GenAI Age (Palani and Ramos)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1145/3635636.3656190](https://doi.org/10.1145/3635636.3656190)
Creative practitioners (like designers, software developers, and architects) have started to employ Generative AI models (GenAI) to produce text, images, and assets comparable to those made by people. While HCI research explores specific GenAI models and creativity support tools, little is known about practitioners’ evolving roles and workflows with GenAI models across a project’s stages. This knowledge is key to guide the development of the new generation of Creativity Support Tools. We contribute to this knowledge by employing a triangulated method to capture interviews, videos, and survey responses of creative practitioners reflecting on projects they completed with GenAI. Our observations let us derive a set of factors that capture practitioners’ perceived roles, challenges, benefits, and interaction patterns when creating with GenAI. From these factors, we offer insights and propose design opportunities and priorities that serve to encourage reflection from the wider community of Creativity Support Tools and GenAI stakeholders such as systems creators, researchers, and educators on how to develop systems that meet the needs of creatives in human-centered ways.

# Examining the Interplay of Efficiency (AI Workplace)

## Summary
Akpan and Adebayo examine what they term the "dual paradoxes" of AI: AI simultaneously increases efficiency while consuming more resources, and augments human capabilities while displacing traditional labor roles. Drawing on published research and industry analysis, they develop a framework for understanding how these paradoxes interact in contemporary workplaces. The paper argues that organizations must grapple with AI's hidden costs—energy consumption, labor dislocation, decision-making ethics—even as they pursue productivity gains.

## Key Concepts
- **Efficiency paradox**: AI improves output per unit of human labor while massively increasing energy and computational resource demands
- **Labor displacement paradox**: AI augments some human roles while substituting for others, creating hybrid roles and eliminating traditional ones
- **Decision ethics**: Ethical dimensions of delegating consequential decisions to AI systems
- **Hybrid human-AI roles**: New categories of work where humans provide oversight, contextual judgment, and error correction for AI systems

## Theoretical Framework
Conceptual analysis grounded in organizational theory and HCI literature. The "dual paradox" framing draws on Jevons Paradox (efficiency improvements increase total consumption) applied to AI in organizational contexts.

## Methods
Conceptual analysis synthesizing published empirical research and industry data on AI deployment, energy use, and labor market outcomes.

## Main Arguments
1. Efficiency gains from AI come with substantial hidden costs in energy and carbon footprint rarely accounted for in ROI calculations
2. AI does not simply substitute for labor—it reconfigures work, creating new hybrid roles while eliminating others
3. Organizations risk ethical failures by delegating decisions to AI systems without adequate accountability structures
4. Sustainable AI adoption requires balancing efficiency goals against resource costs, labor equity, and ethical accountability

## Limitations
Conceptual paper without primary empirical data. The "paradox" framing may oversimplify complex organizational dynamics that vary substantially by sector.

# Formative Study on GenUI Tools (Chen et al. Google DeepMind)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1145/3715336.3735780](https://doi.org/10.1145/3715336.3735780)
AI can now generate high-fidelity UI mock-up screens from a high-level textual description, promising to support UX practitioners’ work. However, it remains unclear how UX practitioners would adopt such Generative UI (GenUI) models in a way that is integral and beneficial to their work. To answer this question, we conducted a formative study with 37 UX-related professionals that consisted of four roles: UX designers, UX researchers, software engineers, and product managers. Using a state-of-the-art GenUI tool, each participant went through a week-long, individual mini-project exercise with role-specific tasks, keeping a daily journal of their usage and experiences with GenUI, followed by a semi-structured interview. We report findings on participants’ workflow using the GenUI tool, how GenUI can support all and each specific roles, and existing gaps between GenUI and users’ needs and expectations, which lead to design implications to inform future work on GenUI development.

## Summary
Chen, Knearem, and Li report a formative study with 37 UX-related professionals (designers, researchers, developers, and PMs) using a generative UI tool over one week, revealing how different roles adopt AI-generated prototypes differently and where significant gaps remain. The study finds that GenUI accelerates early ideation but struggles to fit professional workflows, especially for researchers and developers whose tasks are less prototype-centric. Their design implications push toward role-aware GenUI tools that integrate into existing UX workflows rather than replacing them.

## Key Concepts
- Generative UI (GenUI) — AI that creates high-fidelity UI mockups from text prompts
- Role-differentiated adoption (UXD vs. UXR vs. PM vs. developer)
- Workflow integration vs. workflow disruption
- Design iteration acceleration
- Prompt-to-prototype paradigm

## Theoretical Framework
Human-centered computing with an empirical HCI orientation; uses diary studies and semi-structured interviews to surface workflow-level phenomena rather than testing a specific theoretical model.

## Methods
Formative study: 37 professionals across four UX roles each completed a week-long individual mini-project using a GenUI tool, kept daily journals, and participated in a semi-structured interview afterward.

## Main Arguments
- GenUI accelerates early-stage prototyping but creates friction when integrated into iterative, collaborative workflows
- Different UX roles have fundamentally different relationships to prototypes, making a one-size-fits-all GenUI tool problematic
- Existing GenUI tools underserve UX researchers and developers who need more than visual mockups
- Effective GenUI requires better mechanisms for communicating design intent, not just generating outputs

## Limitations & Critiques
Study was conducted within a single large software company with a state-of-the-art but unnamed GenUI tool, limiting generalizability across organizations and tools; participants were not representative of independent designers or small studios.

# Fostering AI Ethics via Constructionist Pedagogy (Lin and Dai CUHK)

## Summary
Lin and Dai present a constructionist pedagogical approach for developing epistemic insights into AI ethics among upper primary students. Three theory-informed activities have students build and interact with rule-based, ML-based, and generative AI systems, using mathematical reasoning to reflect on fairness, bias, and transparency. The interdisciplinary approach — spanning computer science, mathematics, philosophy, and humanities — helps students understand how AI knowledge construction differs from human cognition, grounding ethical reasoning in epistemic insight rather than abstract principles.

## Key Concepts
- Constructionist AI ethics pedagogy
- Epistemic insights (how AI acquires/processes knowledge)
- K-12 AI ethics education
- Hands-on AI model building
- Fairness, bias, transparency as ethical concepts

## Theoretical Framework
Constructionism (Papert) combined with interdisciplinary AI literacy frameworks; distinguishes between AI literacy (broad) and epistemic insight (understanding how AI processes knowledge differently from humans); uses hands-on building to make abstract concepts concrete.

## Methods
Design-based curriculum implementation at AAAI 2025; three classroom activities with upper primary students; qualitative analysis of student reasoning and artifacts; guided reflection integrated throughout.

## Main Arguments
- Students can develop meaningful epistemic insight into AI — not just use AI tools — when curriculum explicitly scaffolds understanding of how AI learns and processes information
- Constructionist making (building AI models) is more effective than discussing AI abstractly for building ethical reasoning grounded in technical understanding
- An interdisciplinary approach spanning CS, mathematics, and humanities is necessary because AI ethics genuinely requires all three domains
- Students who understand how AI knows things differently from humans can better evaluate AI outputs critically

## Limitations
- Short-term intervention; long-term effects on ethical reasoning unknown
- Requires teacher preparation and curriculum infrastructure not widely available in K-12 settings

Links to [[Epistemic Insights AI Ethics via Constructionism (Lin and Dai CUHK)]] (companion paper by same authors); relates to [[Integrating Unplugged and Plugged for Holistic AI Education (Dai)]] on holistic AI pedagogy; connects to [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] on constructivist theory.

# Fr om code to collaboration:

## Summary
Rastogi and Pandita (Symbiosis Institute of Business Management, Pune) examine IT professionals' perceptions of AI's impact on workforce dynamics through a qualitative study of 27 specialists at multinational corporations. Using thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews, the study finds that IT workers experience AI as simultaneously enabling and threatening: AI streamlines repetitive coding and documentation tasks but creates anxiety about skill obsolescence and role ambiguity. The paper argues that organizations must invest in continuous reskilling, build psychological safety, and redesign work to leverage human-AI complementarity.

## Key Concepts
- **AI-driven workflow reconfiguration**: AI tools change how knowledge work is structured and distributed within teams
- **Skill obsolescence anxiety**: IT professionals' fear that AI will render their existing expertise less valuable
- **Role ambiguity**: Uncertainty about how AI adoption will redefine job responsibilities and performance expectations
- **Human-AI complementarity**: Humans and AI are most productive when their respective strengths are combined
- **Psychological safety**: Organizational climate where workers feel safe to experiment with and adapt to AI tools

## Theoretical Framework
Qualitative organizational behavior research drawing on technology acceptance, organizational change, and human-AI interaction frameworks. Thematic analysis grounds findings in participants' lived experiences.

## Methods
Purposive sampling of 27 IT specialists from multinational corporations; in-depth semi-structured interviews; thematic analysis following systematic coding procedures.

## Main Arguments
1. IT professionals see AI as a productivity tool but fear it will commoditize their specialized skills over time
2. Successful AI integration requires organizational interventions beyond tool deployment: leadership communication, reskilling infrastructure, and participatory role redesign
3. Effective human-AI collaboration requires new meta-skills (AI literacy, prompt engineering, output validation) that current training programs do not provide
4. AI's impacts on workforce dynamics are socially shaped by organizational context, not technologically determined

## Limitations
Single-industry study (IT sector); findings may not transfer to less digitally mature sectors. Purposive sampling limits representativeness. Qualitative findings cannot be generalized to statistical populations.

## Connections
- Connects to [[Transforming Software Development with Generative AI]] on empirical GenAI impacts in software teams
- Relates to [[AI Hasnt Fixed Teamwork Longitudinal Study (CMU MIT Stanford Emory)]] on AI and team dynamics
- Pairs with [[Embracing the AIautomation age]] on strategic HRM for AI adoption

# From Expert Systems to Generative Artificial Experts (Sowa and Przegalinska)

**DOI:** [10.1109/EMR.2023.3272799](https://doi.org/10.1109/EMR.2023.3272799)

## Summary
Sowa and Przegalinska trace the conceptual and technical evolution from classical expert systems of the 1970s-80s to contemporary generative AI, arguing that the latter represents a qualitative shift toward what they term "Generative Artificial Experts" — systems capable of producing contextually appropriate expert-level outputs without explicit rule encoding. The paper examines the epistemic and organizational implications of this shift, particularly for how humans understand, trust, and delegate to AI systems in professional contexts.

## Key Concepts
- Expert systems (MYCIN, XCON paradigm)
- Generative AI as expert knowledge production
- Generative Artificial Experts
- Tacit vs. explicit knowledge in AI systems
- Human-AI delegation and trust in professional contexts

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on knowledge management theory (Polanyi's tacit/explicit distinction), organizational sociology of expertise, and AI systems history; frames the evolution from rule-based to generative AI as a transition in the epistemic structure of machine intelligence.

## Methods
Conceptual and historical analysis; comparative review of expert systems and generative AI capabilities; draws on case examples from professional domains (medicine, law, engineering).

## Main Arguments
- Classical expert systems encoded explicit rules from human experts, making their reasoning transparent but brittle and domain-limited
- Generative AI systems derive performance from statistical patterns in vast data, producing flexible outputs but with opaque reasoning — a fundamentally different epistemic structure
- "Generative Artificial Experts" are emerging as organizational actors whose outputs organizations treat as expert judgment, raising new accountability and governance questions
- Human-AI collaboration models must evolve to account for the different trust calibration challenges posed by each type of system

## Limitations
- "Generative Artificial Expert" as a category is the authors' theoretical contribution — empirical validation of how organizations actually treat GenAI outputs as expert judgment is limited
- Historical framing of expert systems may oversimplify a heterogeneous research tradition

## Connections
Relates to [[Rethinking AI in Organization and Management (Ramaul et al.)]] on theorizing AI in organizations; links to [[Automate Infomate Two Faces of Intelligent Technology (Zuboff 1985)]] on technology and knowledge transformation; connects to [[Beyond Design and Use Studying Intelligent Technologies (Bailey and Barley)]] on evolving AI in organizational contexts.

# GenAI in UX Education: Critical Thinking Assessment (Naing et al.)

**DOI:** [10.1108/IJILT-07-2024-0141](https://doi.org/10.1108/IJILT-07-2024-0141)

## Summary
Naing et al. investigate how generative AI integration in UX education contexts affects students' development of critical thinking competencies. The study examines whether AI tool use scaffolds or undermines students' ability to evaluate design decisions, reason about user needs, and identify gaps in AI-generated outputs. Findings reveal that without structured critical thinking assessment frameworks, students tend to uncritically accept AI outputs, particularly in early design phases, while more structured reflection prompts can mitigate this tendency.

## Key Concepts
- Critical thinking in UX education
- GenAI in design studio courses
- Assessment of AI-mediated learning
- Scaffolded reflection for AI tool use
- UX design student competency development

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on critical thinking frameworks (Paul-Elder model), UX design pedagogy literature, and human-AI interaction research; positions critical thinking as a developmental competency that must be explicitly assessed and scaffolded in AI-integrated design curricula.

## Methods
Empirical study of UX design students using generative AI tools in coursework; assessment instruments measuring critical thinking dimensions (analysis, evaluation, synthesis) before and after structured reflection interventions; comparison across conditions.

## Main Arguments
- Generative AI tool use in UX education has a default tendency to suppress critical engagement — students readily adopt AI suggestions without systematic evaluation
- Structured reflection prompts and critical thinking rubrics can substantially improve students' ability to interrogate AI outputs and identify their limitations
- Assessment must evolve beyond artifact quality to include the reasoning process through which students evaluate and adapt AI-generated work
- Faculty who have not developed their own critical AI practices struggle to model or assess them effectively with students

## Limitations
- Study context is specific to UX design education; critical thinking dynamics may differ in other design disciplines or at different educational levels
- Short-term intervention; longitudinal tracking of critical thinking development in AI-integrated curricula is needed

## Connections
Relates to [[Conceptions of Design Practice (Lotsos et al. Northwestern)]] on design student development; links to [[Tracing the Invisible Students Judgment in AI Design Work (Naik et al. Purdue)]] on student judgment in AI-assisted design; connects to [[Educating for Design Character (Boling Gray Smith)]] on holistic design education.

# Generative AI Integrated Educational Model for User-Centered

## Summary
Wu, Zeng, and Lin (Chengyi College, Jimei University, China) develop and empirically test an educational model integrating ChatGPT and Midjourney into a user-centered design (UCD) curriculum. Grounded in design thinking theory, the model deploys generative AI during both divergent (ideation, visual exploration) and convergent (selection, refinement) design phases. Empirical findings indicate that the AI-integrated curriculum enhanced students' creativity and problem-solving skills compared to traditional instruction.

## Key Concepts
- **User-Centered Design (UCD)**: Design methodology centering user needs, behaviors, and goals throughout the design process
- **Design thinking phases**: Divergent (empathize, define, ideate) and convergent (prototype, test) stages with distinct AI tool applications
- **ChatGPT for text-based ideation**: Used for persona development, scenario writing, problem reframing
- **Midjourney for visual ideation**: Used for rapid concept visualization and design alternative generation
- **AI as cognitive scaffolding**: Lowers barriers to creative ideation while maintaining student ownership of design decisions

## Theoretical Framework
Design thinking theory (Brown/IDEO) combined with educational technology instructional design principles. AI is positioned as scaffolding that extends students' capacity to explore a wider design space.

## Methods
Empirical study comparing AI-integrated and traditional UCD instruction. Pre/post assessment of creativity and problem-solving skills; analysis of student design outputs.

## Main Arguments
1. AI tools can productively scaffold divergent phases of design education by enabling rapid, low-risk ideation
2. Convergent phases require human judgment for selection and critique—AI is a generator, not an arbiter of design quality
3. Integrating AI does not replace design thinking skills but amplifies capacity to explore wider design spaces
4. Structured AI integration (specifying where and how tools are used) outperforms unguided AI experimentation

## Limitations
Single-institution study; Chinese university context may limit generalizability. Creativity measurement in design education is methodologically contested. Specific tools tested (ChatGPT, Midjourney) may become outdated.

## Connections
- Connects to [[Using Generative AI to Support UX Design Students in Web Dev]] on AI in design education

# How to Be Universal: Some Cybernetic Strategies, 1943-70

## Summary
Geof Bowker (1993) analyzes how cybernetics achieved disciplinary expansion and intellectual authority between 1943 and 1970 by strategically constructing universalizing claims about information, feedback, and control. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies, Bowker argues that cybernetics' remarkable cross-disciplinary reach was not simply due to the power of its ideas but resulted from deliberate rhetorical and institutional strategies that positioned cybernetic concepts as universal languages for understanding complex systems across biology, engineering, economics, and the social sciences.

## Key Concepts
- **Universalizing strategies**: Rhetorical and institutional moves that position a local framework as applicable everywhere
- **Boundary objects**: Concepts flexible enough to be adapted across communities while maintaining coherence
- **Feedback and control**: Core cybernetic concepts marketed as universal principles of self-regulating systems
- **Interdisciplinary expansion**: How cybernetics colonized adjacent fields by translating their problems into cybernetic terms
- **The Macy Conferences**: Critical institutional site for constructing and legitimating cybernetic universalism

## Theoretical Framework
Science and Technology Studies (STS), drawing on Latour's actor-network theory and Bowker/Star's work on classification. Cybernetics is analyzed as a social and political project, not merely an intellectual one.

## Methods
Historical analysis of cybernetics' formation using primary sources from Macy Conferences, published works of Wiener, von Neumann, and others, and institutional histories.

## Main Arguments
1. Cybernetics achieved universality not by discovering a genuine universal science but by strategically defining its concepts so broadly that almost any system could be described in cybernetic terms
2. The Macy Conferences were critical sites for constructing and legitimating universalizing claims across disciplines
3. Cybernetic universalism enabled imperial moves—appropriating and reframing other fields' problems in cybernetic language
4. Understanding how universality is constructed is essential for critically evaluating any framework that claims universal applicability

## Limitations
STS analysis may underweight the genuine intellectual contributions of cybernetics. Historical focus on 1943–1970 does not address cybernetics' later decline and transformation into systems theory and complexity science.

## Connections
- Relates to [[Ensmenger - The Rise of Computer Science]] on discipline formation and boundary work in computing
- Situates historical context for AI's current universalizing ambitions
- Connects to [[Orlikowski - Using Technology and Constituting Structures]] on technology as social construction

# HPT Model Applied to Kayak Company (Martin et al.)

**DOI:** [10.1007/978-3-031-77521-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-77521-5)

## Summary
Martin et al. demonstrate the application of the Human Performance Technology (HPT) model to a performance improvement intervention at a kayak manufacturing company. Using Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model and systematic front-end analysis, they identify the root causes of a performance gap in manufacturing processes — finding the primary causes lie in environmental conditions (information, resources, incentives) rather than worker skill deficits. The case illustrates how HPT's systematic needs analysis prevents premature training solutions and leads to more cost-effective, lasting performance improvement.

## Key Concepts
- Human Performance Technology (HPT) model
- Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model (BEM)
- Performance analysis vs. training needs analysis
- Environmental causes of performance gaps
- Front-end analysis

## Theoretical Framework
Gilbert's BEM distinguishes between environmental (information, resources, incentives) and individual (knowledge, capacity, motivation) causes of performance deficits; the HPT model systematically rules out environmental causes before recommending training interventions.

## Methods
Applied case study; performance analysis at a kayak manufacturing company; interviews, observations, and performance data analysis; application of BEM to categorize root causes; intervention design based on findings.

## Main Arguments
- Most performance gaps are caused by environmental factors (unclear expectations, inadequate feedback, insufficient resources) rather than worker skill deficits — training is the wrong solution for environmental causes
- Systematic front-end analysis using HPT prevents the "training reflex" — the tendency to prescribe training without diagnosing root causes
- Environmental interventions (redesigning information flow, clarifying standards, restructuring incentives) produce faster and more durable improvement than training alone
- HPT requires a business-performance orientation, not just an instructional-design orientation

## Limitations
- Single company case study limits generalizability
- HPT analysis depends on access to authentic performance data, which organizations may be reluctant to share or unable to provide accurately

## Connections
Relates to [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] on learning theory foundations of instructional design; connects to [[Activity Theory for Workplace Learning Technologies (Martinez Marroquin and Senadji)]] on technology in work performance contexts; links to broader ID literature on performance consulting.

# Instructional Design and Creativity: A Response to the Criticized

## Summary
Rowland (1995) responds to Dick's defense of Instructional Systems Design (ISD) against critics who argue ISD produces uncreative instruction. Rather than defending creativity as a criterion that should "dominate" (Dick's framing), Rowland argues the debate reveals deeper disagreements about the nature of instructional design itself: whether it is a technical process with predictable outputs or a reflective, creative practice more akin to design than engineering. Rowland challenges the assumption that following high-quality procedures reliably produces high-quality outcomes.

## Key Concepts
- Instructional Systems Design (ISD) creativity debate
- Design vs. engineering models of ID practice
- Reflective practitioner vs. systematic designer
- Creativity as integral to the ID process
- Situated cognition and constructivism in ID

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on design theory, constructivism, and Schön's reflective practice; contrasts the "algorithmic" model of ID (follow the process, get the outcome) with a "designerly" model that sees creative judgment as irreducible; sympathetic to Situated Cognition/Constructivist perspectives that Dick was responding to.

## Methods
Response paper; close analysis of Dick's (1995) arguments; counterargument development through examination of the underlying assumptions about process-outcome relationships in instructional design.

## Main Arguments
- Dick's claim that "ISD methods do result in creative instruction when used appropriately" contains a hidden assumption: that "appropriate use" is specifiable — but what counts as appropriate requires the very creativity being defended
- The debate is not about whether creativity is good but about whether the design of instruction is fundamentally a technical (engineering) or reflective (design) activity
- Process-outcome relationships in design are not predictable in the way Dick assumes — "high-quality procedures" do not guarantee outcomes because design is inherently situated, contextual, and indeterminate
- ISD's strength (systematic process) is also its limitation: it provides structure but can suppress the judgment-based adaptation that characterizes expert design practice

## Limitations
- Written in 1995; the ID field has evolved significantly, with many practitioners now embracing more agile, design-thinking-oriented approaches that partially resolve this debate
- Response format limits the scope of Rowland's own constructive alternative

## Connections
Links to [[Designerly Ways of Knowing (Cross 1982)]] on design vs. science epistemology; relates to [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] on constructivist approaches to instruction; connects to [[Characteristics and Evolution of Foundational Instructional.md]] on ID model development.

# Instructional Design and Creativity: A Response to the Critics

## Summary
Walter Dick's 1995 *Educational Technology* article responds to critics who argue that systematic instructional design stifles creativity. Dick contends that the systematic ID process does not constrain but rather channels creative work: the Dick and Carey model provides a structure within which creative decisions about content, strategies, media, and assessment are made at every stage. Dick distinguishes between the process of design (which should be systematic) and the products of design (which can and should be creative and varied).

## Key Concepts
- **Systematic ID**: A sequenced, iterative process for designing instruction (analyze → design → develop → implement → evaluate)
- **Creativity within constraints**: Creative decisions occur at every step of the ID process, not despite it
- **Design products vs. design process**: The model specifies process, not predetermined outcomes
- **Objectivist vs. constructivist critique**: Critics conflate systematic process with behaviorist outcomes; Dick argues the process is compatible with constructivist goals

## Theoretical Framework
Dick defends a systems-based approach, arguing that systematic process and creative outcomes are not contradictory. He positions the Dick and Carey model as an open framework that accommodates diverse learning theories and innovative solutions within its stages.

## Methods
Conceptual response and defense; draws on experience with the Dick and Carey model and examples of creative ID practice within systematic frameworks.

## Main Arguments
1. Critics misunderstand the Dick and Carey model as prescribing content or strategies when it only prescribes a design process
2. Every step of systematic ID requires creative judgment: choosing objectives, selecting media, devising assessment, etc.
3. Systematic ID is not inherently behaviorist; constructivist outcomes can be pursued within the model
4. The real danger is abandoning systematic process for unguided creativity, which risks ineffective instruction

## Limitations
Dick's defense may understate the degree to which the model's linear logic can constrain iterative, emergent, and participatory design approaches valued by constructivists. The exchange with Rowland reveals genuine paradigmatic disagreement.

- Exchange with [[Instructional Design and Creativity A Response to the Criticized]] (Rowland's rejoinder)

year: 2023
venue: "Computers & Education: Artificial Intelligence"

# Integrating Unplugged and Plugged for Holistic AI Education (Dai)

**DOI:** [10.1007/s10639-024-13043-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-024-13043-w)

## Summary
Dai proposes an "embodied constructionist approach" to AI education that integrates unplugged activities (physical analogies, embodied simulation) with plugged activities (direct interaction with AI systems) to achieve holistic AI literacy. Using design-based research (DBR) over two years with 107 sixth graders, the study implements and refines a cyclical understand–make–reflect process. Students progressively comprehend conceptual, technical, and ethical dimensions of AI through this embodied constructionist framework, outperforming approaches that treat these dimensions separately.

## Key Concepts
- Embodied constructionism (hybrid of embodied cognition + Papert's constructionism)
- Unplugged-plugged integration
- Holistic AI literacy (conceptual + technical + ethical)
- Design-based research (DBR)
- Understand–make–reflect cycle

## Theoretical Framework
Synthesizes embodied cognition theory (Lakoff and Johnson), constructionism (Papert), and AI literacy frameworks (Long and Magerko); argues that physical enactment of AI concepts provides cognitive scaffolding for understanding abstract computational processes.

## Methods
Design-based research over two years; authentic classroom implementation with 107 sixth graders; classroom observation, video-recording, student interviews and artifacts, teacher debriefings; case study analysis of learning trajectories.

## Main Arguments
- Abstract AI concepts require embodied analogies before students can engage meaningfully with plugged AI systems — the unplugged → plugged sequence is pedagogically essential, not merely supplementary
- Holistic AI literacy cannot be achieved by compartmentalizing technical, conceptual, and ethical learning — the embodied constructionist approach integrates all three through making and reflecting
- The understand–make–reflect cycle produces more durable and transferable understanding than linear instruction
- Upper primary school is a critical but under-examined developmental window for AI literacy — age-appropriate pedagogy is distinctively needed

## Limitations
- Two-year DBR study in a single school context; generalizability across curricula, teacher profiles, and cultural contexts requires further investigation
- Embodied constructionist approach demands significant teacher preparation and curriculum redesign
- No comparative group; learning gains are assessed through within-group longitudinal analysis

## Connections
Directly links to [[Epistemic Insights AI Ethics via Constructionism (Lin and Dai CUHK)]] (same research group, complementary approach); relates to [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] on constructivist theory; connects to [[AI Literacy in Design Education Comparative Study (Schauer et al. HTW Berlin)]] on AI literacy pedagogy.
